parts.title: Regression (Classical ML)
parts.blurb: Predict a continuous number from input features. Start here for tabular data before reaching for deep learning.

parts.title: Classification (Classical ML)
parts.blurb: Predict a category label. These are the workhorses for tabular, sensor and hand-crafted-feature data.

parts.title: Ensemble Methods & Gradient Boosting
parts.blurb: Combine many weak models into one strong model. Gradient-boosted trees still win most tabular-data competitions.

parts.title: Clustering (Unsupervised Learning)
parts.blurb: Group similar samples without labels. Used for segmentation, pattern discovery and pre-labelling.

parts.title: Dimensionality Reduction & Manifold Learning
parts.blurb: Compress many features into a few. Used for visualisation, noise removal, speed and feature extraction.

parts.title: Probabilistic & Bayesian Models
parts.blurb: Models that reason with probabilities and uncertainty; the foundation of filtering, speech, and Bayesian ML.

parts.title: Anomaly & Abnormal-Behaviour Detection
parts.blurb: Find rare, unusual events: machine faults, fraud, intrusions, abnormal human behaviour in video. Usually trained on mostly normal data.

parts.title: Time Series & Forecasting
parts.blurb: Predict future values and understand temporal patterns: demand, energy, sensor signals, prices, battery health.

parts.title: Deep Learning Building Blocks
parts.blurb: The basic networks and layers that every deep model is built from.

parts.title: Activation Functions
parts.blurb: Non-linearities that let networks learn complex functions. Choice affects training speed and stability.

parts.title: Loss Functions
parts.blurb: What the network minimises. The right loss encodes what "good" means for your task.

parts.title: Optimisers & Learning-Rate Schedules
parts.blurb: Algorithms that update the weights. Optimiser and schedule choices often matter as much as architecture.

parts.title: Regularisation, Normalisation & Training Tricks
parts.blurb: Techniques that make networks train stably and generalise to new data.

parts.title: CNN Architectures (Image Classification & Backbones)
parts.blurb: Convolutional networks that classify images and serve as feature extractors (backbones) for detection and segmentation.

parts.title: Recurrent & Sequence Models
parts.blurb: Networks with memory for sequences: text, speech, sensor streams, trajectories.

parts.title: Transformers & Large Language Models
parts.blurb: Attention-based models that dominate NLP and increasingly vision, audio and robotics.

parts.title: Classic NLP Algorithms
parts.blurb: Pre-deep-learning text methods that remain fast, cheap baselines.

parts.title: Classical Computer Vision & Image Processing
parts.blurb: Hand-designed image algorithms (mostly OpenCV). Fast, explainable, and still essential for pre-processing, measurement and robotics.

parts.title: Vision Transformers & Vision Foundation Models
parts.blurb: Transformer-based image backbones and large pre-trained models that transfer to almost any vision task.

parts.title: Self-Supervised & Representation Learning
parts.blurb: Learn useful features from unlabelled data, then fine-tune with few labels.

parts.title: Object Detection
parts.blurb: Locate and classify objects with bounding boxes. The workhorse of robotics, surveillance, agriculture and inspection.

parts.title: Image Segmentation
parts.blurb: Classify every pixel: semantic (class per pixel), instance (separate objects) or panoptic (both).

parts.title: Tracking, Pose, Depth & 3D Vision
parts.blurb: Follow objects over time, estimate body and object pose, recover depth and 3-D structure. Core of robot perception.

parts.title: Video Understanding & Action Recognition
parts.blurb: Classify and localise actions and events in video.

parts.title: Generative Models (Images, Data, 3D)
parts.blurb: Models that create new data: images, video, audio, synthetic training data.

parts.title: Multimodal & Vision-Language Models
parts.blurb: Models that connect images, text, audio and more; they power zero-shot vision and visual question answering.

parts.title: Speech & Audio
parts.blurb: Algorithms for speech recognition, synthesis and sound classification.

parts.title: Model Compression, Fine-Tuning & Efficient Deployment
parts.blurb: Make big models smaller, faster and adaptable to your task and hardware.

parts.title: Reinforcement Learning
parts.blurb: Agents learn by trial and error to maximise reward. Used for robot control, games, recommendation and LLM alignment.

parts.title: Robot Learning & Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Models
parts.blurb: Learning-based robot control from demonstrations and foundation models that map images + language to actions.

parts.title: Graph Neural Networks & Graph Algorithms
parts.blurb: Learning on graphs: molecules, social networks, road maps, skeletons, scene graphs, power grids.

parts.title: Recommender Systems
parts.blurb: Predict what users will like: products, videos, courses, papers.

parts.title: Search, Planning & Metaheuristic Optimisation
parts.blurb: Classic AI search, robot path planning and nature-inspired optimisers for problems without gradients.

parts.title: Explainability, Evaluation & Uncertainty
parts.blurb: Understand why a model decides, measure it properly, and know when not to trust it.

parts.title: Learning Paradigms (Semi-, Federated, Meta-, Continual, Active)
parts.blurb: Training strategies for when labels are scarce, data is distributed, or tasks keep changing.

entries.name: Linear Regression (Ordinary Least Squares)
entries.why: Fits a straight line/plane minimising squared error. Fast, interpretable baseline for any numeric prediction.
entries.example: Predict motor temperature from current and ambient temperature.
entries.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = model.predict(X_test)

entries.name: Polynomial Regression
entries.why: Adds powers/interactions of features so a linear model can fit curved relationships.
entries.example: Battery voltage vs. state-of-charge curve fitting.
entries.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
model = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree=3), LinearRegression()).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Ridge Regression (L2)
entries.why: Linear regression with an L2 penalty; shrinks weights to handle multicollinearity and overfitting.
entries.example: Predicting crop yield from many correlated soil sensors.
entries.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
model = Ridge(alpha=1.0).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Lasso Regression (L1)
entries.why: L1 penalty drives some weights to exactly zero, so it also performs feature selection.
entries.example: Finding which of 200 process variables actually affect weld quality.
entries.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso
model = Lasso(alpha=0.1).fit(X, y)
selected = (model.coef_ != 0)

entries.name: Elastic Net
entries.why: Mixes L1 and L2 penalties; stable selection when features come in correlated groups.
entries.example: Genomics or spectroscopy data with thousands of correlated features.
entries.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import ElasticNet
model = ElasticNet(alpha=0.1, l1_ratio=0.5).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Bayesian Ridge Regression
entries.why: Linear regression that returns uncertainty (a distribution over weights), not just a point estimate.
entries.example: Calibration curves where you need confidence bands.
entries.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import BayesianRidge
model = BayesianRidge().fit(X, y)
mean, std = model.predict(X_test, return_std=True)

entries.name: Huber Regression
entries.why: Robust loss: squared for small errors, linear for large ones, so outliers do not dominate.
entries.example: Sensor data with occasional spikes.
entries.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import HuberRegressor
model = HuberRegressor(epsilon=1.35).fit(X, y)

entries.name: RANSAC Regression
entries.why: Repeatedly fits on random subsets and keeps the model with the most inliers; ignores gross outliers.
entries.example: Fitting a floor plane to a LiDAR point cloud.
entries.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import RANSACRegressor
model = RANSACRegressor().fit(X, y)
inliers = model.inlier_mask_

entries.name: Theil-Sen Estimator
entries.why: Median of slopes between point pairs; very robust for small, noisy data.
entries.example: Trend of degradation from a few noisy field measurements.
entries.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import TheilSenRegressor
model = TheilSenRegressor().fit(X, y)

entries.name: Quantile Regression
entries.why: Predicts a chosen percentile (e.g. 90th) instead of the mean; gives prediction intervals.
entries.example: Worst-case delivery-time estimation.
entries.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import QuantileRegressor
q90 = QuantileRegressor(quantile=0.9, alpha=0).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Poisson Regression (GLM)
entries.why: Generalised linear model for count data (non-negative integers).
entries.example: Number of defects per batch, number of calls per hour.
entries.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import PoissonRegressor
model = PoissonRegressor().fit(X, counts)

entries.name: Gamma / Tweedie Regression (GLM)
entries.why: GLMs for positive, skewed targets; Tweedie handles many exact zeros plus a positive tail.
entries.example: Insurance claim amounts, rainfall totals.
entries.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import TweedieRegressor
model = TweedieRegressor(power=1.5, link="log").fit(X, y)

entries.name: Partial Least Squares (PLS) Regression
entries.why: Projects X and y into latent components that maximise covariance; works when features greatly outnumber samples.
entries.example: NIR spectroscopy to predict moisture content.
entries.code:
from sklearn.cross_decomposition import PLSRegression
model = PLSRegression(n_components=5).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Principal Component Regression
entries.why: PCA first, then linear regression on the components; removes collinearity.
entries.example: Regression on highly correlated vibration features.
entries.code:
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
model = make_pipeline(PCA(10), LinearRegression()).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Support Vector Regression (SVR)
entries.why: Fits a tube of width epsilon around the data; kernels give non-linear fits on small/medium data.
entries.example: Predicting tool wear from cutting-force features.
entries.code:
from sklearn.svm import SVR
model = SVR(kernel="rbf", C=10, epsilon=0.1).fit(X, y)

entries.name: k-Nearest Neighbours Regression
entries.why: Prediction = average of the k closest training samples. No training phase; good local model.
entries.example: Estimating house price from similar nearby houses.
entries.code:
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor
model = KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=5).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Decision Tree Regression
entries.why: Splits the feature space into boxes with constant predictions; captures non-linearity and is easy to explain.
entries.example: Rule-like energy-consumption prediction.
entries.code:
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
model = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=5).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Gaussian Process Regression
entries.why: Non-parametric Bayesian model; gives a full predictive distribution. Ideal for small data and Bayesian optimisation.
entries.example: Modelling robot joint friction from a few experiments.
entries.code:
from sklearn.gaussian_process import GaussianProcessRegressor
from sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels import RBF, WhiteKernel
gp = GaussianProcessRegressor(kernel=RBF() + WhiteKernel()).fit(X, y)
mu, sigma = gp.predict(X_test, return_std=True)

entries.name: Kernel Ridge Regression
entries.why: Ridge regression in a kernel feature space; closed-form non-linear regression.
entries.example: Smooth surrogate model of a simulation.
entries.code:
from sklearn.kernel_ridge import KernelRidge
model = KernelRidge(kernel="rbf", alpha=0.1).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Isotonic Regression
entries.why: Fits a monotonic (never decreasing) step function; also used to calibrate classifier probabilities.
entries.example: Dose-response curves; probability calibration.
entries.code:
from sklearn.isotonic import IsotonicRegression
iso = IsotonicRegression().fit(x, y)

entries.name: LOESS / LOWESS (Local Regression)
entries.why: Fits many small weighted regressions to draw a smooth trend through noisy data.
entries.example: Smoothing a noisy temperature log for visual analysis.
entries.code:
from statsmodels.nonparametric.smoothers_lowess import lowess
smoothed = lowess(y, x, frac=0.2)

entries.name: Spline Regression (Splines / GAM)
entries.why: Piecewise polynomials joined smoothly; Generalised Additive Models add one smooth curve per feature.
entries.example: Non-linear effect of age and income on risk, each kept interpretable.
entries.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import SplineTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
model = make_pipeline(SplineTransformer(n_knots=8), Ridge()).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Least Angle Regression (LARS)
entries.why: Efficient path algorithm for high-dimensional linear models; computes the whole Lasso path cheaply.
entries.example: Fast exploration of feature importance when features greatly outnumber samples.
entries.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import Lars
model = Lars(n_nonzero_coefs=10).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Orthogonal Matching Pursuit
entries.why: Greedy sparse regression: picks the most correlated feature step by step. Used in sparse coding.
entries.example: Recovering a sparse signal in compressed sensing.
entries.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import OrthogonalMatchingPursuit
omp = OrthogonalMatchingPursuit(n_nonzero_coefs=5).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Symbolic Regression
entries.why: Searches for an explicit mathematical formula that fits the data (via genetic programming).
entries.example: Rediscovering a physical law from experimental measurements.
entries.code:
from pysr import PySRRegressor
model = PySRRegressor(niterations=40, binary_operators=["+", "*", "-", "/"])
model.fit(X, y)

entries.name: Logistic Regression
entries.why: Linear model producing class probabilities via the sigmoid/softmax. Strong, interpretable baseline.
entries.example: Pass/fail prediction for a manufactured part.
entries.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X, y)
proba = clf.predict_proba(X_test)

entries.name: Perceptron
entries.why: The original single-neuron linear classifier (1958); updates weights only on mistakes.
entries.example: Teaching example; linearly separable sensor thresholds.

entries.name: k-Nearest Neighbours (k-NN) Classifier
entries.why: Labels a sample by majority vote of its k closest neighbours. Simple and effective on small, low-dimensional data.
entries.example: Classifying fruit ripeness from colour features.
entries.code:
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
clf = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Support Vector Machine (SVM)
entries.why: Finds the maximum-margin boundary; kernels (RBF, polynomial) make it non-linear. Excellent on small/medium data.
entries.example: HOG + SVM pedestrian detection; fault classification from vibration features.
entries.code:
from sklearn.svm import SVC
clf = SVC(kernel="rbf", C=1.0, gamma="scale", probability=True).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Linear SVM
entries.why: SVM without a kernel; scales to millions of samples and very wide sparse features.
entries.example: Text classification on TF-IDF vectors.
entries.code:
from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC
clf = LinearSVC(C=1.0).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Gaussian Naive Bayes
entries.why: Assumes features independent and Gaussian per class. Extremely fast; works with tiny datasets.
entries.example: Quick baseline for sensor-based activity classification.
entries.code:
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
clf = GaussianNB().fit(X, y)

entries.name: Multinomial Naive Bayes
entries.why: Naive Bayes for word counts; the classic spam filter.
entries.example: Spam/ham email filtering; complaint-ticket routing.
entries.code:
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
clf = MultinomialNB().fit(X_counts, y)

entries.name: Bernoulli Naive Bayes
entries.why: Naive Bayes for binary (present/absent) features.
entries.example: Short-text classification using word presence.
entries.code:
from sklearn.naive_bayes import BernoulliNB
clf = BernoulliNB().fit(X_binary, y)

entries.name: Complement Naive Bayes
entries.why: Variant of multinomial NB that is more stable on imbalanced text classes.
entries.example: Classifying rare categories of support tickets.
entries.code:
from sklearn.naive_bayes import ComplementNB
clf = ComplementNB().fit(X_counts, y)

entries.name: Decision Tree (CART)
entries.why: Learns if-then rules by splitting on the most informative feature (Gini/entropy). Fully explainable.
entries.example: Machine fault diagnosis rules a technician can read.
entries.code:
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text
clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4).fit(X, y)
print(export_text(clf))

entries.name: ID3 / C4.5 Decision Trees
entries.why: Historic tree algorithms using information gain (ID3) and gain ratio with pruning (C4.5). Basis of modern trees.
entries.example: Teaching tree induction; categorical-data rule mining.

entries.name: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)
entries.why: Assumes Gaussian classes with shared covariance; gives a linear boundary and a supervised dimensionality reduction.
entries.example: EEG motor-imagery classification in brain-computer interfaces.
entries.code:
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis
lda = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=2).fit(X, y)
X2 = lda.transform(X)

entries.name: Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA)
entries.why: Like LDA but each class has its own covariance, so boundaries are curved.
entries.example: Classes with very different spreads, e.g. normal vs. faulty vibration.
entries.code:
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis
clf = QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis().fit(X, y)

entries.name: Nearest Centroid Classifier
entries.why: Assigns each sample to the class with the closest mean. Tiny memory, good with very few examples.
entries.example: Prototype-based classification on embedded features.
entries.code:
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestCentroid
clf = NearestCentroid().fit(X, y)

entries.name: Ridge Classifier
entries.why: Treats classification as ridge regression on +/-1 targets; very fast and robust.
entries.example: Quick linear baseline for many-class problems.
entries.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeClassifier
clf = RidgeClassifier().fit(X, y)

entries.name: SGD Classifier (Online Linear Models)
entries.why: Trains linear SVM/logistic models with stochastic gradient descent; handles streaming and huge data.
entries.example: Online learning on a live sensor stream.
entries.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import SGDClassifier
clf = SGDClassifier(loss="log_loss")
clf.partial_fit(X_batch, y_batch, classes=[0, 1])

entries.name: Passive-Aggressive Classifier
entries.why: Online algorithm that stays passive when correct and updates aggressively when wrong.
entries.example: Real-time news/fake-news stream classification.
entries.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import PassiveAggressiveClassifier
clf = PassiveAggressiveClassifier().fit(X, y)

entries.name: Gaussian Process Classifier
entries.why: Bayesian non-parametric classifier with calibrated uncertainty; for small datasets.
entries.example: Safety-critical classification where confidence matters.
entries.code:
from sklearn.gaussian_process import GaussianProcessClassifier
clf = GaussianProcessClassifier().fit(X, y)

entries.name: Multi-Layer Perceptron Classifier (sklearn)
entries.why: A small feed-forward neural network in scikit-learn; quick non-linear model for tabular data.
entries.example: Classifying gestures from IMU features.
entries.code:
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
clf = MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(64, 32), max_iter=500).fit(X, y)

entries.name: One-vs-Rest / One-vs-One Strategy
entries.why: Turns any binary classifier into a multi-class one by training one model per class (OvR) or per pair (OvO).
entries.example: Multi-class defect types with a binary SVM.
entries.code:
from sklearn.multiclass import OneVsRestClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC
clf = OneVsRestClassifier(SVC()).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Classifier Chains (Multi-label)
entries.why: Predicts several labels at once, feeding each prediction into the next to capture label correlations.
entries.example: Tagging an image with multiple attributes.
entries.code:
from sklearn.multioutput import ClassifierChain
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
chain = ClassifierChain(LogisticRegression()).fit(X, Y)

entries.name: Label Propagation / Label Spreading
entries.why: Semi-supervised: spreads a few known labels through a similarity graph to unlabelled points.
entries.example: Labelling a large image set when only 1% is annotated.
entries.code:
from sklearn.semi_supervised import LabelSpreading
model = LabelSpreading(kernel="knn", n_neighbors=7).fit(X, y_with_minus1)

entries.name: Self-Training Classifier
entries.why: Semi-supervised wrapper: trains, labels confident unlabelled samples, retrains.
entries.example: Growing a defect dataset from a small labelled seed.
entries.code:
from sklearn.semi_supervised import SelfTrainingClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC
model = SelfTrainingClassifier(SVC(probability=True)).fit(X, y_with_minus1)

entries.name: Probability Calibration (Platt / Isotonic)
entries.why: Makes predicted probabilities trustworthy (a predicted 0.8 really means about 80%).
entries.example: Risk scoring where thresholds depend on probabilities.
entries.code:
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC
clf = CalibratedClassifierCV(LinearSVC(), method="sigmoid").fit(X, y)

entries.name: Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating)
entries.why: Trains copies of a model on bootstrap samples and averages them; reduces variance.
entries.example: Stabilising an unstable decision tree.
entries.code:
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingClassifier
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
clf = BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(), n_estimators=100).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Random Forest
entries.why: Bagging of trees plus random feature subsets at each split. Robust, little tuning, gives feature importance.
entries.example: Predictive maintenance, crop-disease risk from weather features.
entries.code:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, n_jobs=-1).fit(X, y)
importance = rf.feature_importances_

entries.name: Extra Trees (Extremely Randomized Trees)
entries.why: Like random forest but split thresholds are random too; faster and often less variance.
entries.example: Fast tabular baseline with many noisy features.
entries.code:
from sklearn.ensemble import ExtraTreesClassifier
clf = ExtraTreesClassifier(n_estimators=300).fit(X, y)

entries.name: AdaBoost
entries.why: Trains weak learners in sequence, up-weighting samples the previous ones got wrong. Powered Viola-Jones face detection.
entries.example: Haar-feature face detection; simple boosted classifiers.
entries.code:
from sklearn.ensemble import AdaBoostClassifier
clf = AdaBoostClassifier(n_estimators=200).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM)
entries.why: Each new tree fits the residual errors (gradients) of the current ensemble. Very accurate on tabular data.
entries.example: Demand forecasting with engineered features.
entries.code:
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier
clf = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.05).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Histogram Gradient Boosting
entries.why: scikit-learn's fast boosting that bins features into histograms (LightGBM-style); handles missing values natively.
entries.example: Large tabular datasets with missing sensor readings.
entries.code:
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
clf = HistGradientBoostingClassifier().fit(X, y)

entries.name: XGBoost
entries.why: Regularised, highly optimised gradient boosting; long-time Kaggle champion for structured data.
entries.example: Credit scoring, churn, failure prediction.
entries.code:
import xgboost as xgb
model = xgb.XGBClassifier(n_estimators=500, max_depth=6, learning_rate=0.05)
model.fit(X_train, y_train, eval_set=[(X_val, y_val)])

entries.name: LightGBM
entries.why: Microsoft's leaf-wise, histogram-based boosting; very fast on large data.
entries.example: Click-through-rate prediction on millions of rows.
entries.code:
import lightgbm as lgb
model = lgb.LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=1000, learning_rate=0.03).fit(X, y)

entries.name: CatBoost
entries.why: Yandex's boosting with built-in categorical feature handling (ordered target statistics); strong defaults.
entries.example: Tabular data with many categorical columns (city, product, vendor).
entries.code:
from catboost import CatBoostClassifier
model = CatBoostClassifier(iterations=1000, verbose=0)
model.fit(X, y, cat_features=["city", "vendor"])

entries.name: NGBoost (Natural Gradient Boosting)
entries.why: Boosting that predicts a full probability distribution, giving uncertainty with each prediction.
entries.example: Forecasting with confidence intervals.
entries.code:
from ngboost import NGBRegressor
model = NGBRegressor().fit(X, y)
dist = model.pred_dist(X_test)

entries.name: Voting Ensemble
entries.why: Combines different model types by majority (hard) or averaged probability (soft) vote.
entries.example: Merging SVM, random forest and logistic regression for a robust classifier.
entries.code:
from sklearn.ensemble import VotingClassifier
vote = VotingClassifier([("lr", lr), ("rf", rf), ("svc", svc)], voting="soft").fit(X, y)

entries.name: Stacking (Stacked Generalisation)
entries.why: A meta-model learns how best to combine the predictions of base models.
entries.example: Competition-winning blends of boosting and neural nets.
entries.code:
from sklearn.ensemble import StackingClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
stack = StackingClassifier([("rf", rf), ("svc", svc)], final_estimator=LogisticRegression()).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Blending
entries.why: Simpler stacking: the meta-model is trained on a held-out set of base-model predictions.
entries.example: Quick ensembling of models trained by different team members.
entries.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
P_hold = np.column_stack([m.predict_proba(X_hold)[:, 1] for m in models])
meta = LogisticRegression().fit(P_hold, y_hold)

entries.name: Rotation Forest
entries.why: Each tree is trained on PCA-rotated feature subsets, increasing diversity and accuracy.
entries.example: Hyperspectral/remote-sensing classification.
entries.code:
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
# core idea: a different PCA rotation on random feature groups for each tree
tree = make_pipeline(PCA(), DecisionTreeClassifier()).fit(X[:, feats], y)

entries.name: Random Subspace Method
entries.why: Random subspace trains each model on a random subset of features; useful when features greatly outnumber samples.
entries.example: High-dimensional spectral data.
entries.code:
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingClassifier
clf = BaggingClassifier(base, max_features=0.5, bootstrap=False).fit(X, y)

entries.name: TabNet
entries.why: Deep learning for tabular data using sequential attention to choose features at each step; interpretable masks.
entries.example: Tabular problems where you want a neural model with feature attributions.
entries.code:
from pytorch_tabnet.tab_model import TabNetClassifier
clf = TabNetClassifier()
clf.fit(X_train, y_train, eval_set=[(X_val, y_val)])

entries.name: TabPFN
entries.why: A transformer pre-trained on millions of synthetic datasets; classifies small tables in one forward pass without training.
entries.example: Instant strong baseline on datasets with up to about 10k rows.
entries.code:
from tabpfn import TabPFNClassifier
clf = TabPFNClassifier().fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = clf.predict(X_test)

entries.name: k-Means
entries.why: Splits data into k groups around centroids by minimising within-cluster distance. Fast and simple.
entries.example: Customer segmentation; colour quantisation of images.
entries.code:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
km = KMeans(n_clusters=5, n_init="auto").fit(X)
labels = km.labels_

entries.name: k-Means++ Initialisation
entries.why: Smart seeding that spreads the first centroids apart; gives better and faster k-means.
entries.example: Default seeding in scikit-learn k-means.
entries.code:
from sklearn.cluster import kmeans_plusplus
centers, idx = kmeans_plusplus(X, n_clusters=5)

entries.name: Mini-Batch k-Means
entries.why: k-means on small random batches; clusters millions of points quickly.
entries.example: Building a visual-word vocabulary from millions of SIFT descriptors.
entries.code:
from sklearn.cluster import MiniBatchKMeans
km = MiniBatchKMeans(n_clusters=1000, batch_size=4096).fit(descriptors)

entries.name: Bisecting k-Means
entries.why: Repeatedly splits the largest cluster in two; builds a hierarchy and is more stable than plain k-means.
entries.example: Document clustering.
entries.code:
from sklearn.cluster import BisectingKMeans
labels = BisectingKMeans(n_clusters=8).fit_predict(X)

entries.name: k-Medoids (PAM)
entries.why: Like k-means but cluster centres are real data points; robust to outliers and works with any distance.
entries.example: Clustering GPS stops with a custom distance metric.
entries.code:
from sklearn_extra.cluster import KMedoids
labels = KMedoids(n_clusters=4, metric="manhattan").fit_predict(X)

entries.name: Fuzzy C-Means
entries.why: Soft clustering: each point gets a membership degree for every cluster.
entries.example: MRI tissue segmentation where boundaries are blurry.
entries.code:
import skfuzzy as fuzz
cntr, u, *_ = fuzz.cluster.cmeans(X.T, c=3, m=2.0, error=1e-5, maxiter=300)

entries.name: Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering
entries.why: Merges closest clusters bottom-up into a tree (dendrogram); no need to fix k in advance.
entries.example: Grouping fault signatures; building taxonomies.
entries.code:
from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering
labels = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=4, linkage="ward").fit_predict(X)

entries.name: Divisive Hierarchical Clustering (DIANA)
entries.why: Top-down: starts with one cluster and repeatedly splits. Good for finding a few large groups.
entries.example: Top-level grouping of product categories.
entries.code:
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, fcluster
Z = linkage(X, method="ward")   # dendrogram, cut top-down
labels = fcluster(Z, t=3, criterion="maxclust")

entries.name: DBSCAN
entries.why: Density-based: finds arbitrarily shaped clusters and labels sparse points as noise. No k required.
entries.example: Clustering LiDAR points into obstacles; GPS hotspot detection.
entries.code:
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN
labels = DBSCAN(eps=0.3, min_samples=10).fit_predict(points)       # -1 = noise

entries.name: HDBSCAN
entries.why: Hierarchical DBSCAN that copes with clusters of varying density; usually the best density clusterer.
entries.example: Clustering embeddings of images or text.
entries.code:
from sklearn.cluster import HDBSCAN
labels = HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=15).fit_predict(X)

entries.name: OPTICS
entries.why: Orders points by reachability to reveal density structure at many scales.
entries.example: Spatial data with nested dense regions.
entries.code:
from sklearn.cluster import OPTICS
labels = OPTICS(min_samples=10).fit_predict(X)

entries.name: Mean Shift
entries.why: Moves each point uphill on the density estimate until it reaches a mode; number of clusters is automatic.
entries.example: Image segmentation; the basis of CamShift tracking.
entries.code:
from sklearn.cluster import MeanShift, estimate_bandwidth
ms = MeanShift(bandwidth=estimate_bandwidth(X)).fit(X)

entries.name: Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM / EM)
entries.why: Models data as a mix of Gaussians fitted with Expectation-Maximisation; soft, elliptical clusters with probabilities.
entries.example: Background subtraction (MOG); speaker modelling.
entries.code:
from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, covariance_type="full").fit(X)
probs = gmm.predict_proba(X)

entries.name: Bayesian Gaussian Mixture (Dirichlet Process)
entries.why: GMM that switches off unneeded components, so it effectively learns the number of clusters.
entries.example: Clustering when the number of modes is unknown.
entries.code:
from sklearn.mixture import BayesianGaussianMixture
bgm = BayesianGaussianMixture(n_components=10, weight_concentration_prior_type="dirichlet_process").fit(
    X)

entries.name: Expectation-Maximisation (EM) Algorithm
entries.why: General recipe for fitting models with hidden variables: alternate guessing hidden values (E) and refitting (M).
entries.example: GMMs, HMM training (Baum-Welch), missing-data imputation.

entries.name: Spectral Clustering
entries.why: Clusters using eigenvectors of a similarity graph; finds non-convex shapes like rings and moons.
entries.example: Image segmentation (normalised cuts); community detection.
entries.code:
from sklearn.cluster import SpectralClustering
labels = SpectralClustering(n_clusters=3, affinity="nearest_neighbors").fit_predict(X)

entries.name: Affinity Propagation
entries.why: Points exchange messages to elect exemplars; the number of clusters emerges automatically.
entries.example: Picking representative images from a collection.
entries.code:
from sklearn.cluster import AffinityPropagation
ap = AffinityPropagation().fit(X)
exemplars = ap.cluster_centers_indices_

entries.name: BIRCH
entries.why: Builds a compact clustering-feature tree in one pass; scales to very large data with little memory.
entries.example: Streaming clustering of log events.
entries.code:
from sklearn.cluster import Birch
labels = Birch(n_clusters=10).fit_predict(X)

entries.name: Self-Organizing Map (SOM / Kohonen)
entries.why: Neural grid that maps high-dimensional data onto 2-D while preserving neighbourhoods; good for visual exploration.
entries.example: Visualising process states of a plant.
entries.code:
from minisom import MiniSom
som = MiniSom(10, 10, X.shape[1], sigma=1.0, learning_rate=0.5)
som.train_random(X, 5000)

entries.name: Co-Clustering (Biclustering)
entries.why: Clusters rows and columns at the same time to find sub-matrices with consistent patterns.
entries.example: Gene-condition analysis; user-item blocks.
entries.code:
from sklearn.cluster import SpectralCoclustering
model = SpectralCoclustering(n_clusters=5).fit(data_matrix)

entries.name: Silhouette / Elbow Method (choosing k)
entries.why: Evaluation tools for picking the number of clusters: inertia elbow and silhouette score.
entries.example: Deciding how many customer segments to use.

entries.name: Deep Embedded Clustering (DEC)
entries.why: Learns an autoencoder embedding and cluster assignments together; clusters images or text better than k-means on raw pixels.
entries.example: Unsupervised grouping of product photos.
entries.code:
import torch
# q_ij: Student-t soft assignment; target p_ij sharpens q; minimise KL(P||Q)
q = 1.0 / (1.0 + torch.cdist(z, mu) ** 2); q = q / q.sum(1, keepdim=True)
p = (q ** 2 / q.sum(0)); p = p / p.sum(1, keepdim=True)
loss = torch.nn.functional.kl_div(q.log(), p, reduction="batchmean")

entries.name: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
entries.why: Finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance; the default linear compression and denoising tool.
entries.example: Eigenfaces; compressing 100 sensor channels into 5 components.
entries.code:
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
pca = PCA(n_components=0.95).fit(X)        # keep 95% variance
Z = pca.transform(X)

entries.name: Incremental PCA
entries.why: PCA computed batch by batch for data that does not fit in memory.
entries.example: PCA on a huge image dataset streamed from disk.

entries.name: Kernel PCA
entries.why: Non-linear PCA using a kernel trick; unfolds curved structures.
entries.example: Denoising images; non-linear feature extraction.
entries.code:
from sklearn.decomposition import KernelPCA
Z = KernelPCA(n_components=2, kernel="rbf", gamma=0.1).fit_transform(X)

entries.name: Sparse PCA
entries.why: PCA with sparse loadings, so each component uses only a few original features; easier to interpret.
entries.example: Identifying which sensors drive each mode of variation.
entries.code:
from sklearn.decomposition import SparsePCA
Z = SparsePCA(n_components=5, alpha=1).fit_transform(X)

entries.name: Truncated SVD (LSA)
entries.why: SVD that works directly on sparse matrices; known as Latent Semantic Analysis for text.
entries.example: Reducing TF-IDF matrices for document similarity.
entries.code:
from sklearn.decomposition import TruncatedSVD
Z = TruncatedSVD(n_components=100).fit_transform(tfidf_matrix)

entries.name: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)
entries.why: Factorises any matrix into U S V^T; the maths behind PCA, recommenders, compression and least squares.
entries.example: Image compression by keeping top singular values.
entries.code:
import numpy as np
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False)
A_k = U[:, :k] @ np.diag(S[:k]) @ Vt[:k]

entries.name: Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
entries.why: Separates mixed signals into statistically independent sources (blind source separation).
entries.example: Removing eye-blink artifacts from EEG; the cocktail-party problem.
entries.code:
from sklearn.decomposition import FastICA
S = FastICA(n_components=3).fit_transform(mixed_signals)

entries.name: Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF)
entries.why: Factorises non-negative data into additive parts; components are interpretable.
entries.example: Topic modelling; separating spectra; parts-based face features.
entries.code:
from sklearn.decomposition import NMF
W = NMF(n_components=10, init="nndsvda").fit_transform(X_nonneg)

entries.name: Factor Analysis
entries.why: Models observed variables as latent factors plus per-feature noise.
entries.example: Psychometrics; reducing survey questions to traits.
entries.code:
from sklearn.decomposition import FactorAnalysis
Z = FactorAnalysis(n_components=3).fit_transform(X)

entries.name: Dictionary Learning / Sparse Coding
entries.why: Learns a set of basis atoms so each signal is a sparse combination of them.
entries.example: Image denoising and super-resolution with learned patches.
entries.code:
from sklearn.decomposition import MiniBatchDictionaryLearning
codes = MiniBatchDictionaryLearning(n_components=100, alpha=1).fit_transform(patches)

entries.name: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA, topic model)
entries.why: Probabilistic topic model: each document is a mix of topics, each topic a mix of words.
entries.example: Discovering themes in maintenance logs or research abstracts.
entries.code:
from sklearn.decomposition import LatentDirichletAllocation
lda = LatentDirichletAllocation(n_components=10).fit(X_counts)

entries.name: t-SNE
entries.why: Non-linear 2-D/3-D embedding that keeps local neighbours together; the classic tool to visualise clusters.
entries.example: Visualising CNN feature embeddings of a dataset.
entries.code:
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE
Z = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30).fit_transform(features)

entries.name: UMAP
entries.why: Faster than t-SNE, better at preserving global structure, and can transform new data.
entries.example: Visualising single-cell data or embedding spaces.
entries.code:
import umap
Z = umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.1).fit_transform(X)

entries.name: Isomap
entries.why: Preserves geodesic distances along the data manifold; unrolls a "Swiss roll".
entries.example: Recovering pose parameters from images.
entries.code:
from sklearn.manifold import Isomap
Z = Isomap(n_neighbors=10, n_components=2).fit_transform(X)

entries.name: Locally Linear Embedding (LLE)
entries.why: Keeps each point's reconstruction from its neighbours; captures non-linear manifolds.
entries.example: Face-pose manifolds.
entries.code:
from sklearn.manifold import LocallyLinearEmbedding
Z = LocallyLinearEmbedding(n_neighbors=10, n_components=2).fit_transform(X)

entries.name: Laplacian Eigenmaps (Spectral Embedding)
entries.why: Embeds the data using eigenvectors of a neighbourhood graph Laplacian.
entries.example: Pre-step of spectral clustering; graph visualisation.
entries.code:
from sklearn.manifold import SpectralEmbedding
Z = SpectralEmbedding(n_components=2).fit_transform(X)

entries.name: Multidimensional Scaling (MDS)
entries.why: Places points in low dimension so pairwise distances match a given distance matrix.
entries.example: Mapping perceptual similarity between products.
entries.code:
from sklearn.manifold import MDS
Z = MDS(n_components=2, dissimilarity="precomputed").fit_transform(D)

entries.name: PaCMAP / TriMap
entries.why: Modern visualisation methods balancing local and global structure; robust alternatives to t-SNE/UMAP.
entries.example: Exploring large embedding sets.
entries.code:
import pacmap
Z = pacmap.PaCMAP(n_components=2).fit_transform(X)

entries.name: Random Projection
entries.why: Projects onto random directions; distances are approximately preserved (Johnson-Lindenstrauss). Very cheap.
entries.example: Fast approximate nearest-neighbour hashing.
entries.code:
from sklearn.random_projection import GaussianRandomProjection
Z = GaussianRandomProjection(n_components=256).fit_transform(X)

entries.name: Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA)
entries.why: Finds projections of two datasets that are maximally correlated.
entries.example: Linking image features with text features; multi-sensor fusion.
entries.code:
from sklearn.cross_decomposition import CCA
Xc, Yc = CCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(X, Y)

entries.name: Feature Selection (Filter / Wrapper / Embedded)
entries.why: Keeps only useful features: statistical filters, recursive elimination, or model-based importance.
entries.example: Reducing 500 vibration features to 20 for an embedded device.
entries.code:
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, mutual_info_classif, RFE
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
X_k = SelectKBest(mutual_info_classif, k=20).fit_transform(X, y)
rfe = RFE(LogisticRegression(max_iter=500), n_features_to_select=20).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Autoencoder (as dimensionality reduction)
entries.why: Neural network that compresses input to a small code and reconstructs it; non-linear PCA.
entries.example: Compressing sensor windows before clustering.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
enc = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 16))
dec = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(16, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 784))
loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(dec(enc(x)), x)

entries.name: Bayes' Theorem / Bayesian Inference
entries.why: Updates belief in a hypothesis from evidence: posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior. Core of probabilistic ML.
entries.example: Fault probability given an alarm; spam filtering.
entries.code: posterior = likelihood * prior / evidence

entries.name: Hidden Markov Model (HMM)
entries.why: Models a sequence of hidden states that emit observations. Classic for speech, gestures and activity sequences.
entries.example: Recognising gesture phases from accelerometer data.
entries.code:
from hmmlearn import hmm
model = hmm.GaussianHMM(n_components=4, covariance_type="diag").fit(X_seq)
states = model.predict(X_seq)

entries.name: Viterbi Algorithm
entries.why: Dynamic programming that finds the most likely hidden-state path in an HMM.
entries.example: Decoding phonemes in speech; POS tagging.

entries.name: Forward-Backward / Baum-Welch
entries.why: Computes state probabilities in an HMM (forward-backward) and trains HMM parameters with EM (Baum-Welch).
entries.example: Learning HMM speech models from unlabelled audio.
entries.code:
from hmmlearn import hmm
model = hmm.GaussianHMM(n_components=3, n_iter=100)
model.fit(X)   # Baum-Welch (EM) under the hood

entries.name: Markov Chain
entries.why: Random process where the next state depends only on the current one. Models transitions and steady states.
entries.example: Machine-state reliability modelling; PageRank.
entries.code:
import numpy as np
P = np.array([[0.9, 0.1], [0.3, 0.7]])
state = np.array([1, 0])
for _ in range(50): state = state @ P      # converges to the stationary distribution

entries.name: Conditional Random Field (CRF)
entries.why: Discriminative sequence labeller using neighbouring labels as context; strong for structured tagging.
entries.example: Named-entity recognition; refining segmentation masks.
entries.code:
import sklearn_crfsuite
crf = sklearn_crfsuite.CRF(algorithm="lbfgs", max_iterations=100)
crf.fit(X_feature_dicts, y_tags)

entries.name: Bayesian Network
entries.why: Directed graph of variables with conditional probability tables; supports causal-style reasoning under uncertainty.
entries.example: Medical or machine fault diagnosis from symptoms.
entries.code:
from pgmpy.models import BayesianNetwork
from pgmpy.inference import VariableElimination
bn = BayesianNetwork([("Overheat", "Alarm"), ("Vibration", "Alarm")]).fit(df)
print(VariableElimination(bn).query(["Overheat"], evidence={"Alarm": 1}))

entries.name: Markov Random Field (MRF)
entries.why: Undirected graphical model; encodes that neighbouring variables (pixels) tend to agree.
entries.example: Image denoising and classic segmentation.
entries.code:
# energy E(x) = sum unary(x_i) + lambda * sum_{i~j} [x_i != x_j]
# minimise with ICM, graph cuts, or belief propagation

entries.name: Belief Propagation
entries.why: Message-passing inference on graphical models; exact on trees, approximate (loopy BP) on graphs.
entries.example: Stereo matching; error-correcting decoders.
entries.code: # message from i to j: m_ij(x_j) = sum_{x_i} phi_i(x_i) * psi_ij(x_i, x_j) * prod_{k != j} m_ki(x_i)

entries.name: Markov Chain Monte Carlo (Metropolis-Hastings)
entries.why: Draws samples from a complex distribution by a random walk with accept/reject steps.
entries.example: Bayesian parameter estimation for a physics model.
entries.code:
import numpy as np
x = 0.0; samples = []
for _ in range(10000):
    x_new = x + np.random.normal(0, 0.5)
    if np.log(np.random.rand()) < log_p(x_new) - log_p(x): x = x_new
    samples.append(x)

entries.name: Gibbs Sampling
entries.why: MCMC that samples one variable at a time from its conditional distribution.
entries.example: Training LDA topic models; RBM sampling.

entries.name: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo / NUTS
entries.why: Uses gradients to propose distant, high-acceptance samples; the default sampler in Stan and PyMC.
entries.example: Bayesian regression with many parameters.
entries.code:
import pymc as pm
with pm.Model():
    w = pm.Normal("w", 0, 1, shape=X.shape[1])
    pm.Normal("y", mu=X @ w, sigma=1, observed=y)
    trace = pm.sample()   # NUTS by default

entries.name: Variational Inference
entries.why: Approximates a posterior with a simple distribution by maximising the ELBO; much faster than MCMC.
entries.example: Large Bayesian models; the core of VAEs.
entries.code:
# ELBO = E_q[log p(x, z)] - E_q[log q(z)] -> maximise w.r.t. q's parameters
import pymc as pm
with model: approx = pm.fit(method="advi")

entries.name: Kernel Density Estimation (KDE)
entries.why: Smooth non-parametric estimate of a probability density from samples.
entries.example: Estimating normal operating density for anomaly scoring.
entries.code:
from sklearn.neighbors import KernelDensity
kde = KernelDensity(bandwidth=0.5).fit(X)
log_density = kde.score_samples(X_test)

entries.name: Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)
entries.why: Picks parameters that make the observed data most probable; the principle behind most loss functions.
entries.example: Fitting a Weibull distribution to failure times.
entries.code:
from scipy import stats
shape, loc, scale = stats.weibull_min.fit(failure_times)

entries.name: Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) Estimation
entries.why: MLE plus a prior; equivalent to adding regularisation (L2 = Gaussian prior, L1 = Laplace prior).
entries.example: Regularised parameter estimates with little data.
entries.code: # theta_MAP = argmax log p(data | theta) + log p(theta)

entries.name: Bayesian Optimisation (Gaussian-process based)
entries.why: Optimises expensive black-box functions using a GP surrogate and an acquisition function (EI/UCB).
entries.example: Tuning PID gains or neural-network hyper-parameters with few trials.
entries.code:
from skopt import gp_minimize
result = gp_minimize(objective, dimensions=[(0.0, 10.0), (0.0, 1.0)], n_calls=30)

entries.name: Probabilistic PCA (PPCA)
entries.why: PCA as a probabilistic latent-variable model; handles missing data and gives likelihoods.
entries.example: PCA on sensor data with gaps.
entries.code:
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
pca = PCA(n_components=5).fit(X)
loglik = pca.score_samples(X)    # PPCA log-likelihood per sample

entries.name: Z-Score / 3-Sigma Rule
entries.why: Flags values more than 3 standard deviations from the mean. Simplest statistical anomaly test.
entries.example: Spike detection on a single temperature sensor.
entries.code:
import numpy as np
z = (x - x.mean()) / x.std()
anomalies = np.abs(z) > 3

entries.name: IQR / Tukey Fences (Boxplot Rule)
entries.why: Flags points outside [Q1 - 1.5 IQR, Q3 + 1.5 IQR]; robust to skewed data.
entries.example: Cleaning outliers from production-time data.
entries.code:
import numpy as np
q1, q3 = np.percentile(x, [25, 75]); iqr = q3 - q1
outliers = (x < q1 - 1.5 * iqr) | (x > q3 + 1.5 * iqr)

entries.name: Grubbs' / Generalized ESD Test
entries.why: Statistical hypothesis test that detects one (Grubbs) or several (G-ESD) outliers in roughly normal data.
entries.example: Lab measurement quality control.
entries.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
G = np.max(np.abs(x - x.mean())) / x.std(ddof=1)
n = len(x); t = stats.t.ppf(1 - 0.05 / (2 * n), n - 2)
G_crit = (n - 1) / np.sqrt(n) * np.sqrt(t**2 / (n - 2 + t**2))

entries.name: Mahalanobis Distance
entries.why: Distance that accounts for feature correlations; flags multivariate outliers.
entries.example: Detecting abnormal combinations of pressure and flow.
entries.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial.distance import mahalanobis
VI = np.linalg.inv(np.cov(X.T)); mu = X.mean(0)
scores = [mahalanobis(x, mu, VI) for x in X_test]

entries.name: Elliptic Envelope (Robust Covariance)
entries.why: Fits a robust Gaussian (Minimum Covariance Determinant) and flags points outside the ellipse.
entries.example: Outliers in roughly Gaussian multivariate sensor data.
entries.code:
from sklearn.covariance import EllipticEnvelope
det = EllipticEnvelope(contamination=0.01).fit(X)
pred = det.predict(X_test)   # -1 = anomaly

entries.name: Isolation Forest
entries.why: Anomalies are easier to isolate with random splits, so they get short tree paths. Fast, scales well, no labels.
entries.example: Fraud detection; abnormal machine cycles; network intrusions.
entries.code:
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
iso = IsolationForest(contamination=0.01, random_state=0).fit(X_train)
score = -iso.score_samples(X_test)   # higher = more abnormal

entries.name: Extended Isolation Forest
entries.why: Uses random oblique (sloped) cuts instead of axis-aligned ones, removing artefacts of the original method.
entries.example: Multivariate anomalies with correlated features.
entries.code:
from h2o.estimators import H2OExtendedIsolationForestEstimator
eif = H2OExtendedIsolationForestEstimator(ntrees=100, extension_level=1)

entries.name: Local Outlier Factor (LOF)
entries.why: Compares each point's local density to its neighbours'; finds outliers in regions of varying density.
entries.example: Unusual transactions relative to a customer's local pattern.
entries.code:
from sklearn.neighbors import LocalOutlierFactor
lof = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20, novelty=True).fit(X_train)
pred = lof.predict(X_test)

entries.name: One-Class SVM
entries.why: Learns a boundary around normal data only; anything outside is anomalous.
entries.example: Novelty detection when only healthy-machine data exists.
entries.code:
from sklearn.svm import OneClassSVM
oc = OneClassSVM(kernel="rbf", nu=0.05, gamma="scale").fit(X_normal)
pred = oc.predict(X_test)

entries.name: Support Vector Data Description (SVDD)
entries.why: Finds the smallest hypersphere enclosing normal data; closely related to one-class SVM.
entries.example: Process monitoring in chemical plants.
entries.code:
# minimise R^2 + C * sum(xi_i) s.t. ||phi(x_i) - a||^2 <= R^2 + xi_i
from sklearn.svm import OneClassSVM  # with RBF kernel equivalent to SVDD

entries.name: k-NN Distance Anomaly Score
entries.why: Anomaly score = distance to the k-th nearest normal sample. Simple and surprisingly strong.
entries.example: Image anomaly scoring on deep features (the basis of PatchCore).
entries.code:
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=5).fit(X_normal)
score = nn.kneighbors(X_test)[0].mean(1)

entries.name: HBOS (Histogram-Based Outlier Score)
entries.why: Builds a histogram per feature and multiplies inverse densities; extremely fast for large data.
entries.example: First-pass screening of millions of log records.
entries.code:
from pyod.models.hbos import HBOS
clf = HBOS().fit(X); scores = clf.decision_scores_

entries.name: COPOD / ECOD
entries.why: Parameter-free detectors based on empirical copulas/cumulative distributions; fast and interpretable.
entries.example: Default unsupervised detector on tabular data.
entries.code:
from pyod.models.ecod import ECOD
clf = ECOD().fit(X); labels = clf.labels_

entries.name: PCA Reconstruction Error (Q / T-squared statistics)
entries.why: Normal data is well reconstructed by top components; large residuals signal anomalies. Classic in process monitoring.
entries.example: Statistical process control in manufacturing.
entries.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
pca = PCA(n_components=5).fit(X_normal)
err = ((X_test - pca.inverse_transform(pca.transform(X_test))) ** 2).sum(1)

entries.name: Autoencoder Anomaly Detection
entries.why: Trained only on normal data; anomalies give high reconstruction error.
entries.example: Detecting faulty motor vibration windows or defective product images.
entries.code:
import torch
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    err = ((model(x) - x) ** 2).mean(dim=1)
is_anomaly = err > threshold   # threshold from validation normals

entries.name: LSTM Autoencoder (abnormal sequence detection)
entries.why: Encodes a time window with an LSTM and reconstructs it; abnormal temporal behaviour reconstructs poorly.
entries.example: Abnormal behaviour in machine signals, ECG, or a person's motion trajectory.

entries.name: LSTM Prediction-Error Detector
entries.why: An LSTM forecasts the next values; a large forecast error means abnormal behaviour (used in NASA telemetry, LSTM-NDT).
entries.example: Spacecraft or industrial telemetry anomalies.
entries.code:
pred = lstm_forecaster(window)
err = (pred - actual).abs()
anomaly = err > err_history.mean() + 3 * err_history.std()

entries.name: ConvLSTM Autoencoder (video anomaly)
entries.why: Combines convolution (space) and LSTM (time) to learn normal motion patterns in video.
entries.example: Detecting fights, falls or running in CCTV footage.
entries.code:
# ConvLSTM cell: LSTM gates computed with conv2d instead of matrix multiply
gates = conv(torch.cat([x_t, h_prev], dim=1))
i, f, o, g = gates.chunk(4, dim=1)
c = torch.sigmoid(f) * c_prev + torch.sigmoid(i) * torch.tanh(g)
h = torch.sigmoid(o) * torch.tanh(c)

entries.name: Future-Frame Prediction Anomaly Detection
entries.why: Predicts the next video frame (U-Net + optical-flow constraints); unexpected events are predicted badly.
entries.example: Abnormal event detection on UCSD Ped2 / ShanghaiTech.
entries.code:
pred_frame = generator(prev_frames)
psnr = 10 * torch.log10(1.0 / ((pred_frame - real_frame) ** 2).mean())
anomaly_score = 1 - (psnr - psnr_min) / (psnr_max - psnr_min)

entries.name: Skeleton-Based Anomaly Detection (GEPC / pose sequences)
entries.why: Models normal human pose sequences (e.g. with ST-GCN autoencoders); unusual movements score high. Privacy-friendly.
entries.example: Detecting falls or aggressive behaviour from pose keypoints.
entries.code:
poses = pose_estimator(video)              # (T, joints, 2)
recon = stgcn_autoencoder(poses)
score = ((recon - poses) ** 2).mean()

entries.name: Weakly-Supervised Video Anomaly (MIL Ranking)
entries.why: Uses only video-level labels; multiple-instance learning ranks the most abnormal segment of an abnormal video higher.
entries.example: UCF-Crime: robbery, fighting, accidents in surveillance video.
entries.code:
import torch
# s_abn, s_norm: segment scores for an abnormal and a normal video
loss = torch.relu(1 - s_abn.max() + s_norm.max()) + 8e-5 * ((s_abn[1:] - s_abn[:-1]) ** 2).sum()

entries.name: Variational Autoencoder (VAE) Anomaly Detection
entries.why: Uses reconstruction probability under a VAE; gives a principled probabilistic anomaly score.
entries.example: Network traffic or telemetry anomalies.
entries.code:
recon, mu, logvar = vae(x)
score = ((recon - x) ** 2).sum(1) - 0.5 * (1 + logvar - mu**2 - logvar.exp()).sum(1)

entries.name: Deep SVDD
entries.why: Trains a network to map normal data close to a centre point; distance from the centre is the anomaly score.
entries.example: One-class image anomaly detection.
entries.code:
z = net(x)
loss = ((z - c) ** 2).sum(dim=1).mean()    # c = mean embedding of normal data

entries.name: PatchCore (Industrial Visual Inspection)
entries.why: Stores a memory bank of pre-trained patch features from good parts; defects are patches far from the bank. Strong on MVTec AD.
entries.example: Surface-defect detection on PCBs, castings, textiles with only good samples.
entries.code:
from anomalib.models import Patchcore
from anomalib.engine import Engine
Engine().fit(model=Patchcore(), datamodule=datamodule)

entries.name: PaDiM
entries.why: Fits a Gaussian per patch location on pre-trained CNN features; Mahalanobis distance gives a defect heatmap.
entries.example: Fast, training-free defect localisation.
entries.code:
from anomalib.models import Padim
model = Padim(backbone="resnet18")

entries.name: EfficientAD / FastFlow / STFPM
entries.why: Newer industrial anomaly detectors (student-teacher networks and normalising flows) running in milliseconds.
entries.example: High-speed inline inspection on production lines.
entries.code:
from anomalib.models import EfficientAd
model = EfficientAd()

entries.name: GANomaly / AnoGAN
entries.why: GAN-based detectors: a generator learns normal data; anomalies cannot be reproduced well.
entries.example: Medical-image or X-ray baggage anomalies.
entries.code: # score = ||E(x) - E(G(x))|| : latent-space reconstruction mismatch

entries.name: USAD / OmniAnomaly / Anomaly Transformer
entries.why: Deep multivariate time-series detectors (adversarial AE, stochastic RNN, association-discrepancy transformer).
entries.example: Server-machine monitoring; water-treatment (SWaT) attacks.
entries.code:
# Anomaly Transformer: anomalies show weak association with distant points
score = association_discrepancy(series_attn, prior_attn) * reconstruction_error

entries.name: Matrix Profile (STUMPY)
entries.why: For every subsequence, the distance to its nearest neighbour; peaks are discords (anomalies), valleys are motifs.
entries.example: Finding the one unusual cycle in months of machine data.
entries.code:
import stumpy
mp = stumpy.stump(ts, m=100)
discord_idx = mp[:, 0].argmax()

entries.name: CUSUM (Cumulative Sum Control Chart)
entries.why: Accumulates small deviations to detect a persistent shift in the mean quickly.
entries.example: Detecting slow drift in a production process.

entries.name: EWMA Control Chart
entries.why: Exponentially weighted moving average chart; sensitive to small shifts in quality data.
entries.example: Statistical process control of part dimensions.

entries.name: Page-Hinkley / ADWIN (Concept Drift)
entries.why: Detects when the data distribution changes over time so models can be retrained.
entries.example: Monitoring a deployed model for data drift.

entries.name: Change-Point Detection (PELT / Binary Segmentation)
entries.why: Finds the times when a signal's statistics change.
entries.example: Segmenting machine operating modes; detecting regime changes.
entries.code:
import ruptures as rpt
bkps = rpt.Pelt(model="rbf").fit(signal).predict(pen=10)

entries.name: Seasonal-Hybrid ESD (Twitter AnomalyDetection)
entries.why: Removes seasonality with STL and applies the generalized ESD test on residuals.
entries.example: Anomalies in daily-seasonal web or energy traffic.
entries.code:
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import STL
resid = STL(series, period=24).fit().resid
anomalies = (resid - resid.mean()).abs() > 3 * resid.std()

entries.name: Robust Random Cut Forest (RRCF)
entries.why: Streaming tree ensemble (used in AWS) that scores how much a point changes the tree structure.
entries.example: Real-time anomaly detection on IoT streams.
entries.code:
import rrcf
tree = rrcf.RCTree()
tree.insert_point(point, index=i)
score = tree.codisp(i)

entries.name: Benford's Law Test
entries.why: Checks if leading-digit frequencies follow Benford's distribution; deviations hint at manipulated numbers.
entries.example: Fraud screening of financial ledgers.
entries.code:
import numpy as np
expected = np.log10(1 + 1 / np.arange(1, 10))
first = np.array([int(str(abs(v))[0]) for v in values if v != 0])
observed = np.bincount(first, minlength=10)[1:] / len(first)

entries.name: Moving Average (SMA / WMA)
entries.why: Averages the last N points to smooth noise and show trend. Simplest forecaster and filter.
entries.example: Smoothing noisy encoder speed readings.
entries.code:
import pandas as pd
sma = pd.Series(x).rolling(window=10).mean()

entries.name: Exponential Smoothing (Simple / EWMA)
entries.why: Weighted average with exponentially decaying weights; adapts quickly to recent data.
entries.example: Short-term demand forecast.
entries.code:
import pandas as pd
ewma = pd.Series(x).ewm(alpha=0.3).mean()

entries.name: Holt's Linear Trend Method
entries.why: Exponential smoothing with a trend term; forecasts series that rise or fall steadily.
entries.example: Forecasting growing sales.
entries.code:
from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import ExponentialSmoothing
fit = ExponentialSmoothing(y, trend="add").fit()

entries.name: Holt-Winters (Triple Exponential Smoothing)
entries.why: Adds seasonality to Holt's method; classic for series with daily/weekly/yearly cycles.
entries.example: Monthly electricity load forecasting.
entries.code:
from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import ExponentialSmoothing
fit = ExponentialSmoothing(y, trend="add", seasonal="mul", seasonal_periods=12).fit()
forecast = fit.forecast(12)

entries.name: ETS (Error-Trend-Seasonality State-Space)
entries.why: Statistical framework covering all exponential-smoothing models with likelihood-based selection and intervals.
entries.example: Automatic forecasting for thousands of product series.
entries.code:
from statsmodels.tsa.exponential_smoothing.ets import ETSModel
res = ETSModel(y, error="add", trend="add", seasonal="add", seasonal_periods=7).fit()

entries.name: Autoregressive Model (AR)
entries.why: Predicts the next value as a weighted sum of past values.
entries.example: Modelling vibration signals; spectral estimation.
entries.code:
from statsmodels.tsa.ar_model import AutoReg
res = AutoReg(y, lags=5).fit()

entries.name: ARIMA
entries.why: AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average: differencing removes trend, AR and MA terms capture dynamics. The classic forecaster.
entries.example: Forecasting monthly sales or weekly consumption.
entries.code:
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA
res = ARIMA(y, order=(2, 1, 2)).fit()
forecast = res.forecast(steps=12)

entries.name: SARIMA / SARIMAX
entries.why: ARIMA with seasonal terms and optional external regressors (X).
entries.example: Hourly load forecasting using temperature as an external input.
entries.code:
from statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax import SARIMAX
res = SARIMAX(y, exog=temp, order=(1, 1, 1), seasonal_order=(1, 1, 1, 24)).fit()

entries.name: Auto-ARIMA
entries.why: Automatically searches ARIMA orders using information criteria (AIC).
entries.example: Fast forecasting without manual order selection.
entries.code:
import pmdarima as pm
model = pm.auto_arima(y, seasonal=True, m=12)

entries.name: VAR (Vector Autoregression)
entries.why: Multivariate AR: each variable is predicted from past values of all variables.
entries.example: Joint forecasting of temperature, humidity and power.
entries.code:
from statsmodels.tsa.api import VAR
res = VAR(df).fit(maxlags=5, ic="aic")
forecast = res.forecast(df.values[-res.k_ar:], steps=10)

entries.name: GARCH
entries.why: Models time-varying volatility (variance), not just the mean.
entries.example: Financial risk; volatility of returns.
entries.code:
from arch import arch_model
res = arch_model(returns, vol="GARCH", p=1, q=1).fit()

entries.name: STL Decomposition
entries.why: Splits a series into trend, seasonal and residual parts using LOESS.
entries.example: Understanding seasonality before modelling; anomaly detection on residuals.
entries.code:
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import STL
res = STL(y, period=12).fit()
trend, seasonal, resid = res.trend, res.seasonal, res.resid

entries.name: Fourier Transform (FFT) for Signals
entries.why: Converts a time signal into its frequency spectrum; reveals periodic components.
entries.example: Bearing-fault frequencies in motor vibration; harmonics in current.
entries.code:
import numpy as np
spectrum = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(signal))
freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(signal), d=1 / fs)

entries.name: Short-Time Fourier Transform / Spectrogram
entries.why: FFT over sliding windows, showing how frequency content changes over time.
entries.example: Audio features; non-stationary vibration analysis; CNN input images.
entries.code:
from scipy import signal
f, t, Sxx = signal.spectrogram(x, fs=fs, nperseg=256)

entries.name: Wavelet Transform
entries.why: Multi-resolution time-frequency analysis; captures short transients that the FFT smears out.
entries.example: Detecting impact faults; ECG QRS detection; denoising.
entries.code:
import pywt
coeffs = pywt.wavedec(signal, "db4", level=4)

entries.name: Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD)
entries.why: Adaptively splits a non-linear, non-stationary signal into intrinsic mode functions.
entries.example: Gearbox fault diagnosis.
entries.code:
from PyEMD import EMD
imfs = EMD().emd(signal)

entries.name: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW)
entries.why: Measures similarity between sequences that vary in speed by optimally aligning them.
entries.example: Gesture recognition; matching two welding cycles of different length.
entries.code:
from tslearn.metrics import dtw
distance = dtw(seq_a, seq_b)

entries.name: Kalman Filter
entries.why: Optimal recursive estimator for linear systems with Gaussian noise; fuses prediction and measurement.
entries.example: Robot localisation, GPS/IMU fusion, object tracking (SORT).
entries.code:
# predict
x = F @ x; P = F @ P @ F.T + Q
# update
K = P @ H.T @ np.linalg.inv(H @ P @ H.T + R)
x = x + K @ (z - H @ x); P = (np.eye(len(x)) - K @ H) @ P

entries.name: Extended Kalman Filter (EKF)
entries.why: Kalman filter for non-linear systems via local linearisation (Jacobians).
entries.example: Mobile-robot EKF localisation; drone attitude estimation.
entries.code:
x = f(x, u); P = Fj(x, u) @ P @ Fj(x, u).T + Q
K = P @ Hj(x).T @ np.linalg.inv(Hj(x) @ P @ Hj(x).T + R)
x = x + K @ (z - h(x)); P = (np.eye(n) - K @ Hj(x)) @ P

entries.name: Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF)
entries.why: Propagates sigma points through the non-linear model; more accurate than EKF without Jacobians.
entries.example: Battery state-of-charge estimation; vehicle tracking.
entries.code:
from filterpy.kalman import UnscentedKalmanFilter, MerweScaledSigmaPoints
pts = MerweScaledSigmaPoints(n=4, alpha=0.1, beta=2.0, kappa=0)
ukf = UnscentedKalmanFilter(dim_x=4, dim_z=2, dt=0.1, fx=fx, hx=hx, points=pts)

entries.name: Particle Filter (Sequential Monte Carlo)
entries.why: Represents the belief with weighted samples; handles any non-linearity and multi-modal distributions.
entries.example: Monte Carlo Localisation (AMCL) for robots on a map.
entries.code:
import numpy as np
particles = motion_model(particles, u)
weights *= measurement_likelihood(z, particles); weights /= weights.sum()
idx = np.random.choice(len(particles), len(particles), p=weights)
particles, weights = particles[idx], np.full(len(particles), 1 / len(particles))

entries.name: Complementary Filter
entries.why: Fuses a fast-but-drifting sensor (gyro) with a slow-but-stable one (accelerometer) using high/low-pass blending.
entries.example: Drone or balancing-robot tilt estimation on a microcontroller.
entries.code: angle = alpha * (angle + gyro_rate * dt) + (1 - alpha) * accel_angle

entries.name: Madgwick / Mahony AHRS Filters
entries.why: Lightweight orientation filters fusing gyro, accelerometer and magnetometer into quaternions.
entries.example: IMU orientation on drones and wearables.
entries.code:
from ahrs.filters import Madgwick
q = Madgwick(gyr=gyro, acc=acc, frequency=100.0).Q

entries.name: Prophet
entries.why: Additive model with trend, seasonality and holiday effects; easy forecasting for business series.
entries.example: Daily demand forecasting with festival effects (e.g. Diwali, Pongal).
entries.code:
from prophet import Prophet
m = Prophet(yearly_seasonality=True).fit(df)   # columns ds, y
forecast = m.predict(m.make_future_dataframe(periods=30))

entries.name: Gradient-Boosted Lag Features (Tabular Forecasting)
entries.why: Turns forecasting into regression on lag/rolling features; boosting models often win forecasting competitions (M5).
entries.example: Retail sales forecasting.

df["lag_7"] = df["y"].shift(7); df["roll_mean_7"] = df["y"].shift(1).rolling(7).mean()

model = lgb.LGBMRegressor().fit(df[features].dropna(), df["y"][df[features].notna().all(1)])

entries.name: LSTM Forecasting
entries.why: Recurrent network that learns long-term temporal dependencies; flexible deep forecaster.
entries.example: Remaining-useful-life (RUL) prediction for bearings or batteries.

entries.name: Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN)
entries.why: Causal, dilated 1-D convolutions with residual blocks; parallel training and long memory.
entries.example: Sensor forecasting and classification on edge devices.

conv = nn.Conv1d(c_in, c_out, kernel_size=3, dilation=d, padding=2 * d)
y = conv(x)[..., :-2 * d]   # chomp to keep it causal

entries.name: DeepAR
entries.why: Amazon's probabilistic autoregressive RNN trained across many related series; outputs distributions.
entries.example: Forecasting thousands of SKUs together.

est = DeepAREstimator(freq="D", prediction_length=14, trainer_kwargs={"max_epochs": 10})
predictor = est.train(train_ds)

entries.name: N-BEATS
entries.why: Pure fully-connected deep forecaster with backward/forward residual stacks; interpretable trend/seasonality blocks.
entries.example: Univariate forecasting competitions (M4).
entries.code:

from neuralforecast.models import NBEATS
nf = NeuralForecast(models=[NBEATS(h=12, input_size=48)], freq="M").fit(df)

entries.name: N-HiTS
entries.why: N-BEATS with multi-rate sampling and hierarchical interpolation; better for long horizons and faster.
entries.example: Long-horizon energy forecasting.
entries.code:
from neuralforecast.models import NHITS
model = NHITS(h=96, input_size=480)

entries.name: Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT)
entries.why: Attention-based forecaster mixing static, known-future and observed inputs; gives interpretable variable importance.
entries.example: Multi-horizon demand forecasting with promotions and holidays.
entries.code:
from neuralforecast.models import TFT
model = TFT(h=24, input_size=168)

entries.name: Informer / Autoformer / FEDformer
entries.why: Efficient transformers for long sequences (sparse attention, auto-correlation, frequency-domain blocks).
entries.example: Long-sequence electricity (ETT) forecasting.

from neuralforecast.models import Informer, Autoformer, FEDformer
models = [Informer(h=96, input_size=336), Autoformer(h=96, input_size=336)]

entries.name: PatchTST
entries.why: Splits a series into patches (like ViT) and models each channel independently; strong long-horizon accuracy.
entries.example: Multivariate sensor forecasting.
entries.code:
from neuralforecast.models import PatchTST
model = PatchTST(h=96, input_size=512, patch_len=16)

entries.name: iTransformer
entries.why: Inverts the transformer: each variable becomes a token, so attention captures cross-variable correlations.
entries.example: Multivariate forecasting with many interacting sensors.
entries.code:
from neuralforecast.models import iTransformer
model = iTransformer(h=96, input_size=96, n_series=21)

entries.name: DLinear / NLinear
entries.why: Very simple linear models on decomposed series that rival transformers for long-horizon forecasting.
entries.example: Strong, cheap baseline before trying deep models.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
trend = moving_avg(x); seasonal = x - trend
y = nn.Linear(L, H)(trend) + nn.Linear(L, H)(seasonal)

entries.name: TimesNet
entries.why: Reshapes 1-D series into 2-D by detected periods and uses 2-D convolutions; general model for forecasting, classification and anomalies.
entries.example: Multi-task time-series analysis.
entries.code:
from neuralforecast.models import TimesNet
model = TimesNet(h=24, input_size=96)

entries.name: Time-Series Foundation Models (Chronos, TimesFM, Moirai)
entries.why: Pre-trained on huge time-series corpora; give zero-shot forecasts without training on your data.
entries.example: Quick forecasts for a new sensor with little history.

from chronos import ChronosPipeline

forecast = pipe.predict(torch.tensor(series), prediction_length=24)

entries.name: ROCKET / MiniRocket (Time-Series Classification)
entries.why: Thousands of random convolution kernels plus a linear classifier; state-of-the-art accuracy at very low cost.
entries.example: Classifying motor fault types from current signatures.

from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeClassifierCV
feats = MiniRocket().fit_transform(X_train)
clf = RidgeClassifierCV().fit(feats, y_train)

entries.name: Shapelets
entries.why: Discovers short discriminative subsequences whose presence identifies a class; interpretable.
entries.example: Finding the signature waveform of a fault.
entries.code:

clf = LearningShapelets(n_shapelets_per_size={20: 5}).fit(X, y)

entries.name: InceptionTime / 1-D CNN Classifier
entries.why: Deep 1-D convolution ensembles for time-series classification.
entries.example: Human-activity recognition from wearable IMUs.

net = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv1d(6, 64, 7, padding=3), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv1d(64, 64, 5, padding=2),

entries.name: Granger Causality
entries.why: Tests whether past values of one series improve prediction of another.

grangercausalitytests(df[["vibration", "temperature"]], maxlag=5)

entries.why: Tests whether a series has a unit root (non-stationary) before ARIMA modelling.
entries.example: Deciding how many times to difference a series.
entries.code:
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller
stat, pvalue, *_ = adfuller(y)

entries.name: ACF / PACF Analysis
entries.why: Autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation plots used to choose AR and MA orders and spot seasonality.
entries.example: Identifying a 24-hour cycle in load data.
entries.code:
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf, plot_pacf
plot_acf(y, lags=48); plot_pacf(y, lags=48)

entries.name: Savitzky-Golay Filter
entries.why: Smooths a signal by fitting local polynomials; keeps peak shape better than moving average.
entries.example: Smoothing spectra or trajectories before differentiation.
entries.code:
from scipy.signal import savgol_filter
smooth = savgol_filter(x, window_length=11, polyorder=3)

entries.name: Butterworth / IIR / FIR Digital Filters
entries.why: Remove unwanted frequency bands (low-pass, high-pass, band-pass) from signals.
entries.example: Removing 50 Hz mains noise from sensor data.

clean = filtfilt(b, a, signal)

entries.name: Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP / Feed-Forward Network)
entries.why: Stacked fully-connected layers with non-linear activations; a universal function approximator.
entries.example: Tabular regression; the head of most CNNs; RL policy networks.

mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(in_dim, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64,
    out_dim))

entries.name: Backpropagation
entries.why: Computes gradients of the loss with respect to every weight using the chain rule; how all neural networks learn.
entries.example: Training every model in this book.

optimizer.zero_grad()
loss.backward()       # backpropagation
optimizer.step()

entries.name: Convolution Layer (Conv2d)
entries.why: Slides small learnable filters over an image; shares weights and detects local patterns anywhere.
entries.example: Edge, texture and part detectors in every CNN.

conv = nn.Conv2d(in_channels=3, out_channels=64, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1)

entries.why: Splits a convolution into per-channel (depthwise) plus 1x1 (pointwise); 8-9x fewer computations.

dw = nn.Conv2d(c, c, 3, padding=1, groups=c)
pw = nn.Conv2d(c, c_out, 1)

entries.why: Spaces out kernel taps to enlarge the receptive field without extra parameters or downsampling.

import torch.nn as nn
conv = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, 3, padding=2, dilation=2)

entries.name: Transposed Convolution (Deconvolution)
entries.why: Learnable upsampling layer.

import torch.nn as nn
up = nn.ConvTranspose2d(128, 64, kernel_size=2, stride=2)

entries.why: Learns offsets so the kernel samples irregular positions that follow object shape.

entries.why: Downsamples feature maps, adds translation tolerance, reduces computation.
entries.example: Every classic CNN; global average pooling before the classifier.

import torch.nn as nn
pool = nn.MaxPool2d(2); gap = nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1)

entries.name: Spatial Pyramid Pooling (SPP / SPPF)
entries.why: Pools at several scales and concatenates, giving multi-scale context and fixed-size outputs.
entries.example: SPPF block in YOLOv5/v8/11.

import torch
y1 = maxpool5(x); y2 = maxpool5(y1); y3 = maxpool5(y2)
out = conv1x1(torch.cat([x, y1, y2, y3], dim=1))   # SPPF

entries.why: Adds the input to the block output (x + F(x)), letting gradients flow; made 100+ layer networks trainable.
