entries.name: Dense Connection
entries.why: Each layer receives the concatenated outputs of all earlier layers; strong feature reuse.
entries.example: DenseNet.
entries.code:
import torch
features = [x]
for layer in layers:
    features.append(layer(torch.cat(features, dim=1)))

entries.name: Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) Block
entries.why: Channel attention: learns a weight for each channel from global context.
entries.example: SE-ResNet, EfficientNet, MobileNetV3.
entries.code:
w = torch.sigmoid(fc2(torch.relu(fc1(x.mean((2, 3))))))
x = x * w[:, :, None, None]

entries.name: CBAM (Convolutional Block Attention Module)
entries.why: Channel attention followed by spatial attention; plug-in boost for CNNs.
entries.example: Improving small-object detection or defect classification.
entries.code:
x = x * channel_attention(x)
x = x * spatial_attention(x)       # sigmoid(conv7x7([mean_c(x), max_c(x)]))

entries.name: Embedding Layer
entries.why: Lookup table mapping discrete IDs (words, users, classes) to dense learnable vectors.
entries.example: Word embeddings in NLP; user/item embeddings in recommenders.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
emb = nn.Embedding(num_embeddings=50000, embedding_dim=256)

entries.name: Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM)
entries.why: Two-layer energy-based generative model trained with contrastive divergence; historic pre-training method.
entries.example: Early collaborative filtering (Netflix prize); deep belief networks.
entries.code:
from sklearn.neural_network import BernoulliRBM
rbm = BernoulliRBM(n_components=128, learning_rate=0.05).fit(X_binary)

entries.name: Deep Belief Network (DBN)
entries.why: Stack of RBMs trained greedily layer by layer, then fine-tuned; started the deep-learning revival (2006).
entries.example: Historic digit recognition and feature learning.

entries.name: Hopfield Network
entries.why: Recurrent associative memory that recalls stored patterns from noisy inputs; modern Hopfield = attention.
entries.example: Pattern completion; theory of attention.
entries.code:
import numpy as np
W = sum(np.outer(p, p) for p in patterns); np.fill_diagonal(W, 0)
s = noisy.copy()
for _ in range(10): s = np.sign(W @ s)

entries.name: Radial Basis Function Network (RBFN)
entries.why: One hidden layer of Gaussian units centred on prototypes; fast to train for function approximation.
entries.example: Non-linear system identification and control.
entries.code:
import numpy as np
phi = np.exp(-((X[:, None, :] - centers[None]) ** 2).sum(-1) / (2 * sigma**2))
w = np.linalg.lstsq(phi, y, rcond=None)[0]

entries.name: Extreme Learning Machine (ELM)
entries.why: Random fixed hidden layer; only output weights are solved with least squares. Trains almost instantly.
entries.example: Fast embedded classifiers.
entries.code:
import numpy as np
H = np.tanh(X @ W_rand + b_rand)
beta = np.linalg.pinv(H) @ Y

entries.name: Echo State Network / Reservoir Computing
entries.why: Fixed random recurrent "reservoir"; only a linear readout is trained. Good for chaotic time series.
entries.example: Low-cost sequence prediction.
entries.code:
import numpy as np
for u in inputs:
    h = np.tanh(W_in @ u + W_res @ h); states.append(h)
W_out = np.linalg.lstsq(np.array(states), targets, rcond=None)[0]

entries.name: Spiking Neural Network (SNN)
entries.why: Neurons communicate with discrete spikes over time (leaky integrate-and-fire); very energy efficient on neuromorphic chips.
entries.example: Event-camera processing on Loihi or SpiNNaker.
entries.code:
import snntorch as snn
lif = snn.Leaky(beta=0.9)
spk, mem = lif(input_current, mem)

entries.name: Capsule Network
entries.why: Groups neurons into vectors (capsules) whose orientation encodes pose; dynamic routing between capsules.
entries.example: Viewpoint-robust digit recognition research.

entries.name: Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN)
entries.why: Places learnable spline activation functions on edges instead of fixed activations on nodes; more interpretable fits.
entries.example: Scientific formula discovery; small physics regressions.
entries.code:
from kan import KAN
model = KAN(width=[2, 5, 1], grid=5, k=3)

entries.name: Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN)
entries.why: Adds the residual of a physical differential equation to the loss, so the network obeys physics.
entries.example: Solving heat-transfer or fluid PDEs; estimating unknown physical parameters.
entries.code:
import torch
u = net(torch.cat([x, t], 1))
u_t = torch.autograd.grad(u.sum(), t, create_graph=True)[0]
u_x = torch.autograd.grad(u.sum(), x, create_graph=True)[0]
u_xx = torch.autograd.grad(u_x.sum(), x, create_graph=True)[0]
loss = ((u_t - alpha * u_xx) ** 2).mean() + bc_loss

entries.name: Neural ODE
entries.why: Treats layer depth as continuous time and integrates the hidden state with an ODE solver.
entries.example: Irregularly-sampled time series; continuous dynamics models.
entries.code:
from torchdiffeq import odeint
z_t = odeint(func, z0, t)    # func(t, z) is a neural network

entries.name: Fourier Neural Operator (FNO)
entries.why: Learns mappings between functions in the Fourier domain; solves families of PDEs fast and resolution-independently.
entries.example: Fast fluid-flow or weather surrogate simulations.
entries.code:
import torch
x_ft = torch.fft.rfft2(x)
out_ft = torch.einsum("bixy,ioxy->boxy", x_ft[:, :, :m, :m], weights)

entries.name: Mixture of Experts (MoE)
entries.why: A router sends each token to a few expert sub-networks; huge capacity at low compute per token.
entries.example: Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3, Switch Transformer.
entries.code:
import torch
gate = torch.softmax(router(x), -1)
topv, topi = gate.topk(2, dim=-1)
y = sum(topv[:, k:k+1] * experts_apply(x, topi[:, k]) for k in range(2))

entries.name: Sigmoid
entries.why: Squashes to (0, 1); used for binary outputs and gates (LSTM). Saturates, so avoid in deep hidden layers.
entries.example: Binary classification output; LSTM gates.
entries.code:
import torch
y = torch.sigmoid(x)       # 1 / (1 + exp(-x))

entries.name: Tanh
entries.why: Squashes to (-1, 1), zero-centred. Common in RNNs and bounded action outputs.
entries.example: RL continuous action outputs in [-1, 1].
entries.code:
import torch
y = torch.tanh(x)

entries.name: ReLU
entries.why: max(0, x). Cheap, avoids vanishing gradients; the default for CNNs.
entries.example: Hidden layers of most CNNs and MLPs.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
act = nn.ReLU()

entries.name: Leaky ReLU / PReLU
entries.why: Small slope for negative inputs avoids "dead" ReLU neurons; PReLU learns the slope.
entries.example: GAN discriminators; YOLOv3 backbones.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
act = nn.LeakyReLU(0.1); pact = nn.PReLU()

entries.name: ELU / SELU
entries.why: Smooth negative part pushes mean activations toward zero; SELU self-normalises deep MLPs.
entries.example: Self-normalising networks for tabular data.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
act = nn.SELU()

entries.name: GELU
entries.why: Smooth, probabilistic ReLU (x times Gaussian CDF); standard in transformers.
entries.example: BERT, GPT, ViT feed-forward layers.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
act = nn.GELU()

entries.name: SiLU / Swish
entries.why: x * sigmoid(x); smooth and non-monotonic, often beats ReLU in deep CNNs.
entries.example: EfficientNet, YOLOv5-v11 backbones.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
act = nn.SiLU()

entries.name: Mish
entries.why: x * tanh(softplus(x)); smooth activation that helped YOLOv4.
entries.example: YOLOv4 backbone.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
act = nn.Mish()

entries.name: Softmax
entries.why: Turns a vector of scores into probabilities that sum to 1; multi-class output and attention weights.
entries.example: Classifier output layer; attention in transformers.
entries.code:
import torch
p = torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1)

entries.name: SwiGLU / GeGLU (Gated Linear Units)
entries.why: Gated feed-forward layer: one projection gates another. Standard in modern LLMs.
entries.example: LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral feed-forward blocks.
entries.code:
import torch.nn.functional as F
y = w2(F.silu(w1(x)) * w3(x))

entries.name: Hard-Swish / Hard-Sigmoid
entries.why: Piecewise-linear approximations of swish/sigmoid that are cheap on mobile hardware.
entries.example: MobileNetV3.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
act = nn.Hardswish()

entries.name: Mean Squared Error (MSE / L2 Loss)
entries.why: Average squared error; standard regression loss, heavily penalises large errors.
entries.example: Predicting joint angles or temperature.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
loss = nn.MSELoss()(pred, target)

entries.name: Mean Absolute Error (MAE / L1 Loss)
entries.why: Average absolute error; robust to outliers.
entries.example: Robust regression; image reconstruction.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
loss = nn.L1Loss()(pred, target)

entries.name: Huber / Smooth L1 Loss
entries.why: L2 near zero, L1 for large errors. Robust and smooth; used for bounding-box regression.
entries.example: Faster R-CNN box regression; DQN TD errors.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
loss = nn.SmoothL1Loss(beta=1.0)(pred, target)

entries.name: Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE)
entries.why: Log-loss for binary or multi-label outputs.
entries.example: Defect / no-defect; multi-label tagging.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
loss = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()(logits, targets.float())

entries.name: Categorical Cross-Entropy
entries.why: Standard multi-class classification loss on softmax outputs.
entries.example: ImageNet classification; next-token prediction in LLMs.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
loss = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(label_smoothing=0.1)(logits, labels)

entries.name: Focal Loss
entries.why: Down-weights easy examples so training focuses on hard ones; fixes extreme class imbalance.
entries.example: RetinaNet dense detection; rare-defect classification.
entries.code:
from torchvision.ops import sigmoid_focal_loss
loss = sigmoid_focal_loss(logits, targets, alpha=0.25, gamma=2.0, reduction="mean")

entries.name: Dice Loss
entries.why: Optimises overlap between predicted and true masks; handles small foreground regions.
entries.example: Medical image segmentation (tumours, vessels).
entries.code:
inter = (p * g).sum(); dice = (2 * inter + 1) / (p.sum() + g.sum() + 1)
loss = 1 - dice

entries.name: IoU / GIoU / DIoU / CIoU Loss
entries.why: Box losses based on Intersection-over-Union; GIoU/DIoU/CIoU also handle non-overlapping boxes and aspect ratio.
entries.example: YOLO and DETR box regression.
entries.code:
from torchvision.ops import complete_box_iou_loss, generalized_box_iou_loss
loss = complete_box_iou_loss(pred_boxes, gt_boxes, reduction="mean")

entries.name: Tversky / Lovasz Loss
entries.why: Tversky weights false positives vs. false negatives; Lovasz directly optimises IoU for segmentation.
entries.example: Segmenting thin cracks where missing pixels is costly.
entries.code:
tp = (p * g).sum(); fp = (p * (1 - g)).sum(); fn = ((1 - p) * g).sum()
loss = 1 - tp / (tp + a * fp + b * fn)

entries.name: KL Divergence
entries.why: Measures how one probability distribution differs from another.
entries.example: VAE regulariser; knowledge distillation; PPO trust region.
entries.code:
import torch.nn.functional as F
loss = F.kl_div(F.log_softmax(student / T, -1), F.softmax(teacher / T, -1), reduction="batchmean")

entries.name: Hinge Loss
entries.why: Margin loss used by SVMs; also used for GAN discriminators.
entries.example: Linear SVM training.
entries.code:
import torch
loss = torch.clamp(1 - y * score, min=0).mean()   # y in {-1, +1}

entries.name: Contrastive Loss
entries.why: Pulls embeddings of similar pairs together and pushes dissimilar pairs apart by a margin.
entries.example: Siamese networks for signature verification.
entries.code:
d = (z1 - z2).norm(dim=1)
loss = (same * d**2 + (1 - same) * torch.clamp(margin - d, min=0) ** 2).mean()

entries.name: Triplet Loss
entries.why: Anchor must be closer to a positive than to a negative by a margin.
entries.example: FaceNet face recognition; person re-identification in tracking.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
loss = nn.TripletMarginLoss(margin=0.2)(anchor, positive, negative)

entries.name: InfoNCE / NT-Xent Loss
entries.why: Contrastive loss over a batch: identify the matching pair among many negatives. Powers SimCLR and CLIP.
entries.example: Self-supervised pre-training; image-text alignment.
entries.code:
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
logits = F.normalize(z1, dim=1) @ F.normalize(z2, dim=1).T / tau
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, torch.arange(len(z1)))

entries.name: ArcFace / CosFace (Angular Margin Losses)
entries.why: Adds an angular margin to softmax so face embeddings become highly discriminative.
entries.example: Face recognition and verification systems.
entries.code:
import torch
cos = F.normalize(emb) @ F.normalize(W).T
theta = torch.acos(cos.clamp(-1 + 1e-7, 1 - 1e-7))
logits = s * torch.cos(theta + m * one_hot)

entries.name: CTC Loss (Connectionist Temporal Classification)
entries.why: Trains sequence models when input and output lengths differ and alignment is unknown.
entries.example: Speech recognition; OCR of text lines.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
loss = nn.CTCLoss(blank=0)(log_probs, targets, input_lengths, target_lengths)

entries.name: Perceptual (VGG) Loss
entries.why: Compares deep VGG features instead of pixels, so results look sharper and more natural.
entries.example: Super-resolution; style transfer.
entries.code: loss = ((vgg_features(output) - vgg_features(target)) ** 2).mean()

entries.name: Adversarial (GAN) Loss
entries.why: The generator tries to fool a discriminator that tells real from fake.
entries.example: GANs, image-to-image translation, realistic super-resolution.
entries.code:
import torch.nn.functional as F
d_loss = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(D(real), ones) +
    F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(D(fake.detach()), zeros)
g_loss = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(D(fake), ones)

entries.name: Distribution Focal Loss (DFL)
entries.why: Predicts box edges as discrete distributions; sharper localisation (used in YOLOv8/11; removed in YOLO26).
entries.example: Anchor-free box regression.
entries.code: loss = F.cross_entropy(pred_dist, tl) * wl + F.cross_entropy(pred_dist, tr) * wr

entries.name: Hungarian Matching Loss (Set Prediction)
entries.why: Optimally matches predictions to ground truth one-to-one before computing losses; removes the need for NMS.
entries.example: DETR, RT-DETR, end-to-end detectors.
entries.code:
from scipy.optimize import linear_sum_assignment
rows, cols = linear_sum_assignment(cost_matrix)    # cost = class + L1 + GIoU

entries.name: Center Loss
entries.why: Pulls features of each class toward a learned class centre; makes embeddings compact.
entries.example: Face recognition alongside softmax.
entries.code: loss = ((features - centers[labels]) ** 2).sum(1).mean() / 2

entries.name: Gradient Descent (Batch)
entries.why: Moves weights opposite to the gradient of the full-dataset loss.
entries.example: Small convex problems; teaching.
entries.code: w = w - lr * grad(loss_fn, w)

entries.name: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with Momentum
entries.why: Updates on mini-batches; momentum smooths noisy steps. Still the best generaliser for many CNNs.
entries.example: Training ResNet on ImageNet; YOLO training.
entries.code:
import torch
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.01, momentum=0.9, weight_decay=5e-4, nesterov=True)

entries.name: AdaGrad
entries.why: Per-parameter learning rates that shrink for frequently updated parameters; good for sparse features.
entries.example: Sparse NLP features.
entries.code:
import torch
opt = torch.optim.Adagrad(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)

entries.name: RMSProp
entries.why: Divides the gradient by a running average of its magnitude; works well for RNNs and RL.
entries.example: DQN on Atari; RNN training.
entries.code:
import torch
opt = torch.optim.RMSprop(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

entries.name: Adam
entries.why: Momentum plus adaptive per-parameter scaling; fast, robust default for most deep learning.
entries.example: Training transformers, autoencoders, RL agents.
entries.code:
import torch
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4, betas=(0.9, 0.999))

entries.name: AdamW
entries.why: Adam with decoupled weight decay; the standard optimiser for transformers and LLMs.
entries.example: Fine-tuning BERT, ViT, LLaMA.
entries.code:
import torch
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-4, weight_decay=0.05)

entries.name: Nadam / RAdam
entries.why: Adam with Nesterov momentum (Nadam) or variance rectification for a stable start (RAdam).
entries.example: Drop-in Adam alternatives when early training is unstable.
entries.code:
import torch
opt = torch.optim.RAdam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

entries.name: LAMB / LARS
entries.why: Layer-wise adaptive learning rates that allow very large batch training.
entries.example: BERT pre-training with batch size 32k.
entries.code: # LARS: local_lr = eta * ||w|| / (||grad|| + wd * ||w||)

entries.name: Lion
entries.why: Sign-based optimiser found by program search; less memory than Adam and often comparable or better.
entries.example: Training vision transformers and diffusion models.
entries.code:
from lion_pytorch import Lion
opt = Lion(model.parameters(), lr=1e-4, weight_decay=1e-2)

entries.name: Muon
entries.why: Orthogonalises the momentum update of 2-D weight matrices (Newton-Schulz iteration); trains LLMs faster than AdamW.
entries.example: Speed-run LLM pre-training; used in Kimi K2-style training.
entries.code:
import torch
opt = torch.optim.Muon(hidden_matrix_params, lr=0.02, momentum=0.95)       # PyTorch 2.9+

entries.name: MuSGD
entries.why: Hybrid of SGD and Muon introduced by Ultralytics with YOLO26 for more stable, faster detector training.
entries.example: Training YOLO26 models.
entries.code:
from ultralytics import YOLO
YOLO("yolo26n.yaml").train(data="coco8.yaml", epochs=100)       # optimizer="auto" by default; see
    Ultralytics docs for MuSGD

entries.name: Shampoo / SOAP (Second-Order Preconditioning)
entries.why: Uses matrix preconditioners for faster convergence than diagonal methods like Adam.
entries.example: Large-scale training where wall-clock time matters.
entries.code: # preconditioner: G <- G * L^(-1/4) * R^(-1/4), with L, R running stats of G G^T and G^T G

entries.name: L-BFGS
entries.why: Quasi-Newton method using curvature estimated from recent gradients; very efficient on small, smooth problems.
entries.example: Style transfer optimisation; PINN fine-tuning; logistic regression.
entries.code:
import torch
opt = torch.optim.LBFGS(model.parameters(), lr=1, max_iter=20)
opt.step(closure)

entries.name: Newton's Method / Gauss-Newton / Levenberg-Marquardt
entries.why: Second-order methods; Levenberg-Marquardt is the standard for non-linear least squares.
entries.example: Camera calibration, bundle adjustment, curve fitting.
entries.code:
from scipy.optimize import least_squares
res = least_squares(residual_fn, x0, method="lm")

entries.name: Step / Multi-Step LR Decay
entries.why: Divides the learning rate by a factor at fixed epochs.
entries.example: Classic ResNet training (divide by 10 at epochs 30, 60, 90).
entries.code:
import torch
sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.MultiStepLR(opt, milestones=[30, 60, 90], gamma=0.1)

entries.name: Cosine Annealing (with Warm Restarts)
entries.why: Smoothly decays the learning rate along a cosine curve; restarts help escape poor minima.
entries.example: Modern CNN and ViT training.
entries.code:
import torch
sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(opt, T_max=epochs)

entries.name: Linear Warm-up
entries.why: Starts with a tiny learning rate and ramps up, preventing early instability (critical for transformers).
entries.example: First 1-5% of steps in LLM and ViT training.
entries.code:
import torch
warm = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LinearLR(opt, start_factor=0.01, total_iters=1000)

entries.name: One-Cycle Policy
entries.why: Rises then falls in learning rate (and inverse for momentum) over one cycle; fast convergence.
entries.example: fast.ai-style rapid training.
entries.code:
import torch
sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.OneCycleLR(opt, max_lr=0.01, total_steps=steps)

entries.name: Reduce-LR-on-Plateau
entries.why: Lowers the learning rate when validation loss stops improving.
entries.example: Training without a fixed schedule.
entries.code:
import torch
sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.ReduceLROnPlateau(opt, factor=0.5, patience=5)
sched.step(val_loss)

entries.name: Learning-Rate Range Test (LR Finder)
entries.why: Sweeps learning rate upward over a few batches to find the largest stable value.
entries.example: Picking a learning rate for a new dataset.

entries.name: Dropout
entries.why: Randomly zeroes neurons during training so the network cannot rely on any single one.
entries.example: MLP heads; transformer layers.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
drop = nn.Dropout(p=0.3)

entries.name: DropPath (Stochastic Depth)
entries.why: Randomly skips whole residual blocks during training; regularises very deep networks.
entries.example: ViT, Swin, ConvNeXt training.
entries.code:
from timm.layers import DropPath
x = x + DropPath(0.1)(block(x))

entries.name: DropBlock
entries.why: Drops contiguous regions of feature maps instead of single units; better for convolutions.
entries.example: Regularising detection backbones.
entries.code:
from timm.layers import DropBlock2d
x = DropBlock2d(drop_prob=0.1, block_size=7)(x)

entries.name: L1 / L2 Weight Decay
entries.why: Penalises large weights to reduce overfitting.
entries.example: Almost every training run uses weight decay.
entries.code:
import torch
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), weight_decay=0.01)

entries.name: Early Stopping
entries.why: Stops training when validation performance stops improving; prevents overfitting and saves time.
entries.example: Any supervised training loop.

entries.name: Batch Normalization
entries.why: Normalises activations over the batch; faster, more stable training of CNNs.
entries.example: ResNet, YOLO backbones.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
bn = nn.BatchNorm2d(64)

entries.name: Layer Normalization
entries.why: Normalises across features of each sample; independent of batch size. Standard in transformers and RNNs.
entries.example: Every transformer block.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
ln = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)

entries.name: RMSNorm
entries.why: Simplified LayerNorm (no mean subtraction); cheaper, used in modern LLMs.
entries.example: LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
norm = nn.RMSNorm(d_model)

entries.name: Group / Instance Normalization
entries.why: GroupNorm normalises over channel groups (good for small batches); InstanceNorm per image (style transfer).
entries.example: Detection/segmentation with batch size 2; neural style transfer.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
gn = nn.GroupNorm(num_groups=32, num_channels=256); inorm = nn.InstanceNorm2d(64)

entries.name: Weight Initialisation (Xavier / He)
entries.why: Sets initial weights so signal variance stays stable through layers; He for ReLU, Xavier for tanh.
entries.example: Custom network definitions.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
nn.init.kaiming_normal_(conv.weight, mode="fan_out", nonlinearity="relu")
nn.init.xavier_uniform_(linear.weight)

entries.name: Gradient Clipping
entries.why: Caps the gradient norm to prevent exploding gradients.
entries.example: RNN and transformer training; RL (PPO).
entries.code:
import torch
torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)

entries.name: Label Smoothing
entries.why: Replaces hard 0/1 targets with slightly softened ones; reduces over-confidence.
entries.example: ImageNet training; machine translation.
entries.code:
import torch.nn as nn
loss = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(label_smoothing=0.1)(logits, y)

entries.name: Mixed-Precision Training (AMP, FP16/BF16)
entries.why: Runs most operations in 16-bit to save memory and nearly double speed on modern GPUs.
entries.example: Training large models on an RTX GPU.
entries.code:
import torch
with torch.autocast(device_type="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
    loss = criterion(model(x), y)
loss.backward()

entries.name: Gradient Accumulation
entries.why: Sums gradients over several small batches to simulate a large batch on limited GPU memory.
entries.example: Fine-tuning on a single GPU.

entries.name: Gradient Checkpointing
entries.why: Recomputes activations during the backward pass instead of storing them; big memory savings.
entries.example: Training long-context transformers.
entries.code:
from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint
y = checkpoint(block, x, use_reentrant=False)

entries.name: Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of Weights
entries.why: Keeps a smoothed copy of the weights for evaluation; more stable and accurate models.
entries.example: YOLO training; diffusion models; self-supervised teachers.

entries.name: Data Augmentation (Geometric / Photometric)
entries.why: Random flips, crops, rotations, colour jitter: creates new training samples and improves robustness.
entries.example: Any image classifier or detector.
entries.code:
from torchvision.transforms import v2
aug = v2.Compose([v2.RandomResizedCrop(224), v2.RandomHorizontalFlip(), v2.ColorJitter(0.3, 0.3, 0.3)])

entries.name: Scaled Dot-Product Attention
entries.why: Each token builds its output as a weighted sum of all tokens, weights from query-key similarity. The core of transformers.
entries.example: Inside every transformer layer.

attn = torch.softmax(Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) / Q.size(-1) ** 0.5, dim=-1)
out = attn @ V

entries.name: Multi-Head Attention
entries.why: Runs several attention heads in parallel so each can focus on different relations.
entries.example: BERT, GPT, ViT.

mha = nn.MultiheadAttention(embed_dim=512, num_heads=8, batch_first=True)

entries.name: Transformer (Encoder-Decoder, 2017)
entries.why: "Attention Is All You Need": replaces recurrence with self-attention; parallel training, long-range context.
entries.example: Machine translation; base for all modern LLMs.

entries.name: Positional Encoding (Sinusoidal / Learned)
entries.why: Injects token order information, since attention itself ignores order.
entries.example: Original transformer; BERT (learned).

pos = torch.arange(L).unsqueeze(1); i = torch.arange(0, d, 2)

entries.name: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)
entries.why: Rotates query/key vectors by position-dependent angles; encodes relative position and extends to longer contexts.
entries.example: LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral, GPT-NeoX.

entries.why: Adds a distance-proportional penalty to attention scores instead of embeddings; extrapolates to longer inputs.

entries.why: Several query heads share key/value heads; much smaller KV cache and faster inference.

v = v.repeat_interleave(n_q_heads // n_kv_heads, dim=1)

entries.why: Stores past keys/values so each new token only computes attention for itself; essential for fast generation.

entries.why: A small draft model proposes several tokens; the big model verifies them in one pass. 2-3x faster with identical output.

entries.name: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
entries.why: Retrieves relevant documents and feeds them to the LLM; grounds answers in your own data and reduces hallucination.

entries.why: Prompting or training models to produce step-by-step reasoning before the answer; big gains in maths, logic and planning.

entries.why: Produces sentence vectors whose cosine similarity reflects meaning; basis of semantic search and RAG.

entries.why: Finds similar vectors among millions in milliseconds using graphs (HNSW) or quantised indexes (IVF-PQ).

D, I = index.search(query_vectors, 5)

entries.name: Bag-of-Words (Count Vectoriser)
entries.why: Represents text by word counts, ignoring order. Simple input for linear classifiers.
entries.example: Spam detection baseline.
entries.code:
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
X = CountVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2)).fit_transform(texts)

entries.name: TF-IDF
entries.why: Weights words by frequency in a document times rarity across documents; highlights informative words.
entries.example: Document search; keyword extraction; text classification.
entries.code:
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
X = TfidfVectorizer(max_features=20000, stop_words="english").fit_transform(texts)

entries.name: BM25
entries.why: Probabilistic ranking function improving TF-IDF with term saturation and length normalisation; standard search baseline.
entries.example: Keyword search; hybrid retrieval in RAG.
entries.code:
from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi
bm25 = BM25Okapi([d.split() for d in docs])
scores = bm25.get_scores(query.split())

entries.name: N-gram Language Model (with Smoothing)
entries.why: Predicts the next word from the previous n-1 words using counts; Kneser-Ney smoothing handles unseen n-grams.
entries.example: Keyboard autocomplete; speech recognition language models.
entries.code:
from nltk.lm import KneserNeyInterpolated
from nltk.lm.preprocessing import padded_everygram_pipeline
train, vocab = padded_everygram_pipeline(3, tokenized_sents)
lm = KneserNeyInterpolated(3); lm.fit(train, vocab)

entries.name: Word2Vec (Skip-gram / CBOW)
entries.why: Learns word vectors where similar words are close and analogies are linear (king - man + woman = queen).
entries.example: Feature vectors for words; item2vec for products.
entries.code:
from gensim.models import Word2Vec
w2v = Word2Vec(sentences, vector_size=100, window=5, sg=1)
w2v.wv.most_similar("motor")

entries.name: GloVe
entries.why: Word vectors from global co-occurrence statistics.
entries.example: Pre-trained embeddings for small NLP models.
entries.code:
import gensim.downloader as api
glove = api.load("glove-wiki-gigaword-100")

entries.name: FastText
entries.why: Word vectors built from character n-grams; handles misspellings and unseen words; very fast classifier.
entries.example: Language identification; tagging noisy text.
entries.code:
from gensim.models import FastText
model = FastText(sentences, vector_size=100)

entries.name: Doc2Vec
entries.why: Learns a vector for a whole document alongside word vectors.
entries.example: Document similarity and clustering.
entries.code:
from gensim.models.doc2vec import Doc2Vec, TaggedDocument
model = Doc2Vec([TaggedDocument(d, [i]) for i, d in enumerate(docs)], vector_size=100)

entries.name: Stemming & Lemmatisation
entries.why: Reduces words to a root form (running -> run) so variants are counted together.
entries.example: Pre-processing for search and classical text classifiers.
entries.code:
from nltk.stem import PorterStemmer, WordNetLemmatizer
PorterStemmer().stem("running"); WordNetLemmatizer().lemmatize("better", pos="a")

entries.name: Part-of-Speech Tagging & Named-Entity Recognition (spaCy)
entries.why: Tags each word's grammatical role and finds entities like people, places, organisations.
entries.example: Extracting part numbers and dates from service reports.
entries.code:
import spacy
doc = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")("Replace bearing on KUKA iiwa in Chennai by Monday")
[(e.text, e.label_) for e in doc.ents]

entries.name: Dependency Parsing
entries.why: Finds grammatical relations between words (subject, object, modifier).
entries.example: Turning commands like "pick the red cube" into structured actions.
entries.code:
import spacy
doc = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")("Pick the red cube")
[(t.text, t.dep_, t.head.text) for t in doc]

entries.name: TextRank / Extractive Summarisation
entries.why: PageRank on a sentence-similarity graph; selects the most central sentences.
entries.example: Summarising long reports without generation.
entries.code:
import networkx as nx
scores = nx.pagerank(nx.from_numpy_array(sentence_similarity_matrix))

entries.name: Levenshtein Edit Distance
entries.why: Minimum insertions, deletions and substitutions to turn one string into another.
entries.example: Spell correction; fuzzy matching of OCR output.

entries.name: Sentiment Analysis (VADER Lexicon)
entries.why: Rule- and lexicon-based sentiment scorer tuned for social-media text; no training needed.
entries.example: Quick sentiment of student feedback.
entries.code:
from nltk.sentiment import SentimentIntensityAnalyzer
SentimentIntensityAnalyzer().polarity_scores("The lab session was great!")

entries.name: Grayscale & Colour-Space Conversion (RGB/HSV/LAB)
entries.why: Changes how colour is represented; HSV/LAB separate colour from brightness, making colour thresholds robust to lighting.
entries.example: Detecting red tomatoes or a coloured marker on a conveyor.
entries.code:
import cv2
hsv = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)
mask = cv2.inRange(hsv, (0, 120, 70), (10, 255, 255))

entries.name: Histogram Equalisation
entries.why: Spreads out intensity values to improve global contrast.
entries.example: Enhancing dark X-ray or night images.
entries.code:
import cv2
eq = cv2.equalizeHist(gray)

entries.name: CLAHE (Contrast-Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalisation)
entries.why: Local histogram equalisation with clipping; boosts local contrast without amplifying noise.
entries.example: Medical images; underwater and foggy images; leaf vein enhancement.
entries.code:
import cv2
clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=2.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
out = clahe.apply(gray)

entries.name: Gamma Correction
entries.why: Non-linear brightness adjustment to compensate for camera/display response.
entries.example: Brightening shadows before detection.
entries.code:
import numpy as np
out = (255 * (img / 255.0) ** (1 / 1.8)).astype("uint8")

entries.name: Gaussian Blur
entries.why: Smooths an image with a Gaussian kernel; removes noise before edge detection.
entries.example: Pre-processing for Canny.
entries.code:
import cv2
blur = cv2.GaussianBlur(img, (5, 5), sigmaX=1.0)

entries.name: Median Filter
entries.why: Replaces each pixel with the neighbourhood median; removes salt-and-pepper noise while keeping edges.
entries.example: Cleaning noisy sensor images.
entries.code:
import cv2
out = cv2.medianBlur(img, 5)

entries.name: Bilateral Filter
entries.why: Smooths flat regions while preserving sharp edges by weighting both distance and intensity difference.
entries.example: Cartoon effect; denoising before segmentation.
entries.code:
import cv2
out = cv2.bilateralFilter(img, d=9, sigmaColor=75, sigmaSpace=75)

entries.name: Non-Local Means Denoising
entries.why: Averages similar patches from across the image; strong classical denoiser.
entries.example: Low-light image cleanup.
entries.code:
import cv2
out = cv2.fastNlMeansDenoisingColored(img, None, 10, 10, 7, 21)

entries.name: Unsharp Masking (Sharpening)
entries.why: Adds back the difference between an image and its blur to sharpen details.
entries.example: Enhancing text before OCR.
entries.code:
import cv2
sharp = cv2.addWeighted(img, 1.5, cv2.GaussianBlur(img, (0, 0), 3), -0.5, 0)

entries.name: Global Thresholding
entries.why: Converts grayscale to binary with a fixed cut-off.
entries.example: Segmenting dark parts on a bright backlit table.
entries.code:
import cv2
_, binary = cv2.threshold(gray, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)

entries.name: Otsu's Thresholding
entries.why: Automatically picks the threshold that best separates two intensity classes.
entries.example: Segmenting objects from a uniform background without tuning.
entries.code:
import cv2
_, binary = cv2.threshold(gray, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)

entries.name: Adaptive Thresholding
entries.why: Computes a local threshold for each region; handles uneven lighting.
entries.example: Document scanning; reading labels under shadows.
entries.code:
import cv2
binary = cv2.adaptiveThreshold(gray, 255, cv2.ADAPTIVE_THRESH_GAUSSIAN_C, cv2.THRESH_BINARY, 11, 2)

entries.name: Morphological Operations (Erode, Dilate, Open, Close)
entries.why: Shape-based filters on binary masks: remove specks (open), fill holes (close), thin or thicken shapes.
entries.example: Cleaning a segmentation mask before counting parts.
entries.code:
import cv2, numpy as np
k = np.ones((5, 5), np.uint8)
clean = cv2.morphologyEx(mask, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, k)
filled = cv2.morphologyEx(clean, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, k)

entries.name: Skeletonisation / Thinning
entries.why: Reduces shapes to one-pixel-wide centre lines while keeping topology.
entries.example: Measuring crack length; analysing root or vessel structure.
entries.code:
from skimage.morphology import skeletonize
skel = skeletonize(binary > 0)

entries.name: Sobel / Scharr / Prewitt Edge Operators
entries.why: Approximate image gradients to find edges and their direction.
entries.example: Gradient features; edge magnitude maps.
entries.code:
import cv2
gx = cv2.Sobel(gray, cv2.CV_64F, 1, 0, ksize=3)
gy = cv2.Sobel(gray, cv2.CV_64F, 0, 1, ksize=3)
mag = cv2.magnitude(gx, gy)

entries.name: Laplacian / Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG)
entries.why: Second-derivative operator that highlights rapid intensity changes; LoG also detects blobs.
entries.example: Focus/blur measure (variance of Laplacian); blob detection.
entries.code:
import cv2
sharpness = cv2.Laplacian(gray, cv2.CV_64F).var()    # low = blurry image

entries.name: Canny Edge Detector
entries.why: Multi-stage optimal edge detector: smoothing, gradients, non-maximum suppression, hysteresis thresholding.
entries.example: Lane detection; part outlines for measurement.
entries.code:
import cv2
edges = cv2.Canny(gray, threshold1=50, threshold2=150)

entries.name: Hough Line Transform
entries.why: Votes in parameter space to find straight lines even when broken or noisy.
entries.example: Lane detection; finding the edges of a table or conveyor.
entries.code:
import cv2, numpy as np
lines = cv2.HoughLinesP(edges, 1, np.pi / 180, threshold=80, minLineLength=50, maxLineGap=10)

entries.name: Hough Circle Transform
entries.why: Detects circles of given radius range.
entries.example: Detecting coins, holes, pipes, eye pupils.
entries.code:
import cv2
circles = cv2.HoughCircles(gray, cv2.HOUGH_GRADIENT, dp=1.2, minDist=30, param1=100, param2=30,
    minRadius=10, maxRadius=60)

entries.name: Contour Detection & Shape Analysis
entries.why: Finds object outlines in a binary image, then measures area, perimeter, bounding box, centroid.
entries.example: Counting and measuring parts; pick-point calculation for a robot.
entries.code:
import cv2
contours, _ = cv2.findContours(mask, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
for c in contours:
    M = cv2.moments(c); cx, cy = M["m10"] / M["m00"], M["m01"] / M["m00"]

entries.name: Polygon Approximation (Douglas-Peucker)
entries.why: Simplifies a contour to fewer vertices; classifies shapes (triangle, rectangle).
entries.example: Detecting square markers or box faces.
entries.code:
import cv2
approx = cv2.approxPolyDP(contour, 0.02 * cv2.arcLength(contour, True), True)

entries.name: Convex Hull & Convexity Defects
entries.why: Smallest convex polygon around a shape; defects reveal concavities.
entries.example: Counting fingers in hand-gesture recognition.
entries.code:
import cv2
hull = cv2.convexHull(contour, returnPoints=False)
defects = cv2.convexityDefects(contour, hull)

entries.name: Minimum-Area Rotated Rectangle
entries.why: Tightest rotated box around a contour, giving orientation.
entries.example: Finding grasp angle of a part on a conveyor.
entries.code:
import cv2
(cx, cy), (w, h), angle = cv2.minAreaRect(contour)

entries.name: Image Moments & Hu Moments
entries.why: Statistical shape descriptors; Hu moments are invariant to translation, scale and rotation.
entries.example: Matching shapes regardless of pose.
entries.code:
import cv2
hu = cv2.HuMoments(cv2.moments(contour)).flatten()

entries.name: Connected-Component Labelling
entries.why: Assigns a unique label to each blob of connected foreground pixels, with stats.
entries.example: Counting seeds or pills; removing small noise blobs.
entries.code:
import cv2
n, labels, stats, centroids = cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(mask)

entries.name: Distance Transform
entries.why: For each foreground pixel, distance to the nearest background pixel.
entries.example: Separating touching objects; finding the safest grasp point.
entries.code:
import cv2
dist = cv2.distanceTransform(mask, cv2.DIST_L2, 5)

entries.name: Watershed Segmentation
entries.why: Treats the image as a topographic surface and floods from markers; separates touching objects.
entries.example: Counting touching cells, coins or grains.
entries.code:
import cv2
markers = cv2.watershed(img, markers)

entries.name: GrabCut
entries.why: Iterative graph-cut segmentation from a rough box; separates foreground from background.
entries.example: Interactive product-photo background removal.
entries.code:
import cv2, numpy as np
mask = np.zeros(img.shape[:2], np.uint8); bgd = np.zeros((1, 65)); fgd = np.zeros((1, 65))
cv2.grabCut(img, mask, rect, bgd, fgd, 5, cv2.GC_INIT_WITH_RECT)

entries.name: Graph-Cut / Normalised-Cut Segmentation
entries.why: Formulates segmentation as finding a minimum cut in a pixel graph.
entries.example: Classic interactive and medical segmentation.
entries.code: # energy minimisation: unary data cost + pairwise smoothness, solved by max-flow/min-cut

entries.name: Felzenszwalb Graph-Based Segmentation
entries.why: Fast greedy merging of pixels into regions based on internal variation.
entries.example: Region proposals for Selective Search.
entries.code:
from skimage.segmentation import felzenszwalb
segments = felzenszwalb(img, scale=100, sigma=0.5, min_size=50)

entries.name: SLIC Superpixels
entries.why: Groups pixels into compact, colour-consistent superpixels; reduces later computation.
entries.example: Pre-segmentation for crop and leaf analysis.
entries.code:
from skimage.segmentation import slic
segments = slic(img, n_segments=300, compactness=10)

entries.name: Region Growing
entries.why: Starts from seed pixels and adds neighbours with similar intensity.
entries.example: Segmenting a tumour from a clicked seed point.
entries.code:
from skimage.segmentation import flood
mask = flood(gray, seed_point=(120, 200), tolerance=10)

entries.name: Active Contours (Snakes) / Level Sets
entries.why: A curve evolves to fit object boundaries by minimising an energy.
entries.example: Medical organ boundary refinement.
entries.code:
from skimage.segmentation import active_contour
snake = active_contour(gray_smooth, init_contour, alpha=0.015, beta=10, gamma=0.001)

entries.name: Template Matching
entries.why: Slides a template over the image and finds the best correlation match.
entries.example: Locating a fiducial mark or logo with fixed appearance.
entries.code:
import cv2
res = cv2.matchTemplate(img, templ, cv2.TM_CCOEFF_NORMED)
_, score, _, top_left = cv2.minMaxLoc(res)

entries.name: Harris Corner Detector
entries.why: Finds corners where intensity changes strongly in all directions.
entries.example: Feature points for calibration and tracking.
entries.code:
import cv2, numpy as np
R = cv2.cornerHarris(np.float32(gray), blockSize=2, ksize=3, k=0.04)

entries.name: Shi-Tomasi (Good Features to Track)
entries.why: Improved Harris score; picks the strongest corners for tracking.
entries.example: Initialising Lucas-Kanade optical flow.
entries.code:
import cv2
pts = cv2.goodFeaturesToTrack(gray, maxCorners=200, qualityLevel=0.01, minDistance=10)

entries.name: FAST Corner Detector
entries.why: Very fast corner test on a circle of 16 pixels; ideal for real-time SLAM.
entries.example: Keypoints in ORB-SLAM.
entries.code:
import cv2
kps = cv2.FastFeatureDetector_create(threshold=25).detect(gray)

entries.name: SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform)
entries.why: Keypoints and 128-D descriptors invariant to scale and rotation, robust to lighting. Gold-standard classical features.
entries.example: Image stitching; object recognition; structure-from-motion.
entries.code:
import cv2
sift = cv2.SIFT_create()
kps, desc = sift.detectAndCompute(gray, None)

entries.name: SURF
entries.why: Faster SIFT-like features using box filters and integral images (patented; in opencv-contrib non-free).
entries.example: Historic real-time matching.
entries.code:
import cv2
surf = cv2.xfeatures2d.SURF_create(400)    # requires opencv-contrib with non-free enabled

entries.name: ORB (Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF)
entries.why: Free, fast binary features with rotation invariance; matched with Hamming distance.
entries.example: ORB-SLAM; real-time visual odometry on embedded boards.
entries.code:
import cv2
orb = cv2.ORB_create(nfeatures=1000)
kps, desc = orb.detectAndCompute(gray, None)

entries.name: BRIEF / BRISK / FREAK / AKAZE
entries.why: Binary or non-linear-scale-space descriptors; trade-offs between speed and robustness.
entries.example: Fast matching on mobile robots (AKAZE is free and robust).
entries.code:
import cv2   # OpenCV 4.x
akaze = cv2.AKAZE_create()
kps, desc = akaze.detectAndCompute(gray, None)

entries.name: Feature Matching (Brute-Force / FLANN + Ratio Test)
entries.why: Matches descriptors between images; Lowe's ratio test removes ambiguous matches.
entries.example: Panorama stitching; object localisation.
entries.code:
import cv2
matches = cv2.BFMatcher(cv2.NORM_L2).knnMatch(d1, d2, k=2)
good = [m for m, n in matches if m.distance < 0.75 * n.distance]

entries.name: RANSAC (Random Sample Consensus)
entries.why: Robustly fits a model (line, plane, homography) by repeated random sampling and inlier counting.
entries.example: Homography with outlier matches; plane fitting in point clouds.
entries.code:
import cv2
H, inliers = cv2.findHomography(src_pts, dst_pts, cv2.RANSAC, 5.0)

entries.name: Homography & Perspective Warp
entries.why: 3x3 transform mapping one plane to another; rectifies views.
entries.example: Bird's-eye view of a table for pick-and-place; document scanning.
entries.code:
import cv2
M = cv2.getPerspectiveTransform(src_quad, dst_quad)
top_view = cv2.warpPerspective(img, M, (w, h))

entries.name: Affine Transformations (Rotate, Scale, Shear)
entries.why: Linear warps that keep parallel lines parallel.
entries.example: Data augmentation; aligning images.
entries.code:
import cv2
M = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D(center, angle=30, scale=1.0)
rot = cv2.warpAffine(img, M, (w, h))

entries.name: Image Pyramids & Laplacian Blending
entries.why: Multi-scale image representations; Laplacian pyramids blend images seamlessly.
entries.example: Panorama blending; coarse-to-fine search.
entries.code:
import cv2
down = cv2.pyrDown(img); up = cv2.pyrUp(down)
laplacian = cv2.subtract(img, up)

entries.name: Image Stitching (Panorama)
entries.why: Matches features, estimates homographies and blends images into one panorama.
entries.example: Wide field-of-view inspection; drone mapping.
entries.code:
import cv2
status, pano = cv2.Stitcher_create().stitch([img1, img2, img3])

entries.name: Camera Calibration (Zhang's Method)
entries.why: Estimates camera intrinsics and lens distortion from checkerboard images.
entries.example: Accurate measurement; robot hand-eye setup.
entries.code:
import cv2
ret, K, dist, rvecs, tvecs = cv2.calibrateCamera(obj_pts, img_pts, gray.shape[::-1], None, None)
undist = cv2.undistort(img, K, dist)

entries.name: Hand-Eye Calibration (Tsai-Lenz)
entries.why: Finds the transform between a robot flange and a mounted camera (AX = XB).
entries.example: Eye-in-hand calibration for a KUKA or UR arm.
entries.code:
import cv2   # OpenCV 4.x
R_cam2grip, t_cam2grip = cv2.calibrateHandEye(R_g2b, t_g2b, R_t2c, t_t2c,
    method=cv2.CALIB_HAND_EYE_TSAI)

entries.name: Perspective-n-Point (PnP)
entries.why: Computes camera (or object) pose from known 3-D points and their 2-D image positions.
entries.example: Pose of a marker or known part for robotic grasping; AR.
entries.code:
import cv2
ok, rvec, tvec = cv2.solvePnP(object_points, image_points, K, dist)

entries.name: ArUco / AprilTag Fiducial Markers
entries.why: Square coded markers detected robustly with ID and 6-DoF pose.
entries.example: Robot localisation; calibrating object positions; AR.
entries.code:
import cv2
detector = cv2.aruco.ArucoDetector(cv2.aruco.getPredefinedDictionary(cv2.aruco.DICT_4X4_50))
corners, ids, _ = detector.detectMarkers(gray)

entries.name: Epipolar Geometry (Fundamental / Essential Matrix)
entries.why: Relates corresponding points in two views; recovers relative camera motion.
entries.example: Visual odometry; two-view reconstruction.
entries.code:
import cv2
E, mask = cv2.findEssentialMat(p1, p2, K, method=cv2.RANSAC)
_, R, t, _ = cv2.recoverPose(E, p1, p2, K)

entries.name: Triangulation
entries.why: Recovers a 3-D point from its projections in two calibrated views.
entries.example: Stereo measurement; building sparse 3-D maps.
entries.code:
import cv2
X_h = cv2.triangulatePoints(P1, P2, pts1.T, pts2.T)
X = (X_h[:3] / X_h[3]).T

entries.name: Stereo Block Matching / SGBM (Disparity & Depth)
entries.why: Computes disparity between rectified stereo images; depth = focal x baseline / disparity.
entries.example: Depth sensing for obstacle avoidance.
entries.code:
import cv2
sgbm = cv2.StereoSGBM_create(minDisparity=0, numDisparities=128, blockSize=5)
disparity = sgbm.compute(left_gray, right_gray).astype("float32") / 16

entries.name: Structure from Motion (SfM)
entries.why: Reconstructs camera poses and a 3-D point cloud from many unordered photos.
entries.example: 3-D model of a building or field from drone images (COLMAP).
entries.code:
import pycolmap
pycolmap.extract_features(db_path, image_dir)
pycolmap.match_exhaustive(db_path)
maps = pycolmap.incremental_mapping(db_path, image_dir, output_dir)

entries.name: Bundle Adjustment
entries.why: Jointly refines all camera poses and 3-D points by minimising reprojection error (non-linear least squares).
entries.example: Final optimisation step in SfM and visual SLAM.
entries.code:
from scipy.optimize import least_squares
res = least_squares(reprojection_residuals, x0, jac_sparsity=A, method="trf")

entries.name: Lucas-Kanade Optical Flow (Sparse)
entries.why: Tracks feature points between frames assuming small motion and brightness constancy.
entries.example: Feature tracking; visual odometry; video stabilisation.
entries.code:
import cv2
p1, st, err = cv2.calcOpticalFlowPyrLK(prev_gray, gray, p0, None)

entries.name: Farneback Dense Optical Flow
entries.why: Estimates motion vectors for every pixel using polynomial expansion.
entries.example: Motion maps for action recognition or crowd flow.
entries.code:
import cv2
flow = cv2.calcOpticalFlowFarneback(prev_gray, gray, None, 0.5, 3, 15, 3, 5, 1.2, 0)

entries.name: Horn-Schunck Optical Flow
entries.why: Global dense optical flow with a smoothness constraint; classic variational method.
entries.example: Teaching optical flow; smooth motion fields.
entries.code: # minimise sum (Ix*u + Iy*v + It)^2 + alpha^2 * (|grad u|^2 + |grad v|^2) by iterative updates

entries.name: Background Subtraction (MOG2 / KNN)
entries.why: Models each pixel's background with Gaussian mixtures; moving objects become foreground.
entries.example: Counting vehicles; intrusion detection with a fixed camera.
entries.code:
import cv2
bg = cv2.createBackgroundSubtractorMOG2(history=500, varThreshold=16)
fg_mask = bg.apply(frame)

entries.name: Frame Differencing
entries.why: Subtracts consecutive frames to detect motion; simplest motion detector.
entries.example: Low-cost motion alarm.
entries.code:
import cv2
motion = cv2.absdiff(prev_gray, gray) > 25

entries.name: Mean Shift & CamShift Tracking
entries.why: Tracks a colour histogram by climbing to the density peak; CamShift also adapts size and orientation.
entries.example: Tracking a coloured object or face with a webcam.
entries.code:
import cv2
back = cv2.calcBackProject([hsv], [0], roi_hist, [0, 180], 1)
rot_box, window = cv2.CamShift(back, window, (cv2.TERM_CRITERIA_EPS | cv2.TERM_CRITERIA_COUNT, 10, 1))

entries.name: Correlation-Filter Trackers (MOSSE / KCF / CSRT)
entries.why: Learn a filter in the Fourier domain to track a target at hundreds of FPS.
entries.example: Single-object tracking on embedded hardware.
entries.code:
import cv2
tracker = cv2.TrackerCSRT_create()   # needs opencv-contrib-python
tracker.init(frame, bbox); ok, bbox = tracker.update(next_frame)

entries.name: HOG (Histogram of Oriented Gradients)
entries.why: Describes shape by histograms of edge directions in cells; with an SVM, the classic pedestrian detector.
entries.example: Pedestrian detection; shape features for classical classifiers.

entries.name: LBP (Local Binary Patterns)
entries.why: Encodes texture by comparing each pixel with its neighbours; fast and illumination-robust.
entries.example: Texture classification (fabric, wood defects); face recognition.
entries.code:
from skimage.feature import local_binary_pattern
lbp = local_binary_pattern(gray, P=8, R=1, method="uniform")

entries.name: Haar Cascades (Viola-Jones)
entries.why: Boosted cascade of simple Haar features with integral images; the first real-time face detector (2001).
entries.example: Face and eye detection on low-power devices.

entries.name: Gabor Filters
entries.why: Oriented band-pass filters similar to early visual cortex cells; capture texture at chosen frequency and angle.
entries.example: Fingerprint enhancement; fabric defect detection.
entries.code:

entries.why: Removes duplicate overlapping detections, keeping the highest-scoring box.

entries.name: Breadth-First / Depth-First Search
entries.why: Systematic graph exploration; BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
entries.example: Grid maze solving; connectivity checks.

entries.name: Dijkstra's Algorithm
entries.why: Shortest paths with non-negative edge weights.
entries.example: Route planning on a road or warehouse graph.

entries.name: A* Search
entries.why: Dijkstra guided by a heuristic toward the goal; optimal and much faster with an admissible heuristic.
entries.example: Mobile-robot grid path planning; game pathfinding.
entries.code:
import heapq
f = g[n] + h(n, goal)          # e.g. Euclidean or Manhattan heuristic

entries.name: D* Lite / Theta* / Hybrid A*
entries.why: Variants for replanning in changing maps (D* Lite), any-angle paths (Theta*), and car-like kinematics (Hybrid A*).
entries.example: Rovers replanning around new obstacles; autonomous parking.
entries.code:
# Hybrid A*: expand states (x, y, theta) with motion primitives; heuristic = max(Reeds-Shepp, holonomic
    A*)

entries.name: RRT (Rapidly-exploring Random Tree)
entries.why: Grows a random tree through free space; fast planning in high-dimensional configuration spaces.
entries.example: Robot-arm motion planning around obstacles.

entries.name: RRT* / Informed RRT*
entries.why: Asymptotically optimal RRT that rewires the tree to shorten paths.
entries.example: Smooth, near-optimal manipulator paths (MoveIt / OMPL).
entries.code: # after adding q_new: choose best parent within radius, then rewire neighbours through q_new if cheaper

entries.name: PRM (Probabilistic Roadmap)
entries.why: Samples many free configurations and connects them into a roadmap; answers many queries in the same environment.
entries.example: Repeated planning in a static workcell.
entries.code:
nodes = [sample_free() for _ in range(500)]
edges = [(a, b) for a in nodes for b in knn(a, nodes, 10) if collision_free(a, b)]

entries.name: Potential Fields
entries.why: Goal attracts, obstacles repel; follow the gradient. Simple reactive navigation (local minima possible).
entries.example: Simple obstacle avoidance for small robots.
entries.code:
F = k_att * (goal - p) + sum(k_rep * (1 / d - 1 / d0) / d**2 * (p - o) / d for o, d in obstacles if d <

entries.name: Trajectory Optimisation (CHOMP / TrajOpt)
entries.why: Optimise a whole trajectory for smoothness and obstacle clearance.
entries.example: Smooth arm trajectories in cluttered spaces.
entries.code: # minimise sum ||x_{t+1} - x_t||^2 + lambda * sum obstacle_cost(x_t) by gradient descent

entries.name: Minimax with Alpha-Beta Pruning
entries.why: Optimal play in two-player zero-sum games; alpha-beta skips branches that cannot matter.
entries.example: Chess, tic-tac-toe, Connect-4 engines.

entries.name: Genetic Algorithm (GA)
entries.why: Evolves a population with selection, crossover and mutation; optimises any black-box objective.
entries.example: Scheduling; robot gait parameters; feature selection.
entries.code:
for gen in range(G):
    fitness = np.array([f(ind) for ind in pop])
    parents = pop[np.argsort(-fitness)[:N // 2]]

entries.name: Genetic Programming
entries.why: Evolves programs or formulas (trees) rather than parameter vectors.
entries.example: Symbolic regression; evolving controllers.
entries.code:

model = SymbolicRegressor(population_size=2000, generations=20).fit(X, y)

entries.name: Differential Evolution
entries.why: Population optimiser creating trial vectors from scaled differences of members; robust for continuous problems.
entries.example: Tuning PID gains; fitting model parameters.
entries.code:
from scipy.optimize import differential_evolution
res = differential_evolution(cost, bounds=[(0, 10), (0, 5), (0, 1)])

entries.name: Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO)
entries.why: Particles move under pulls toward their own best and the swarm's best positions.
entries.example: Antenna design; neural-network or controller tuning.
entries.code:
v = w * v + c1 * r1 * (p_best - x) + c2 * r2 * (g_best - x)
x = x + v

entries.name: Ant Colony Optimisation (ACO)
entries.why: Simulated ants lay pheromones on good paths; finds good routes in combinatorial problems.
entries.example: Vehicle routing; travelling salesman; PCB drilling order.
entries.code: prob = (tau[i] ** alpha) * (eta[i] ** beta); prob[visited] = 0; prob /= prob.sum()

entries.name: Simulated Annealing
entries.why: Accepts worse moves with a probability that shrinks as "temperature" cools; escapes local optima.
entries.example: Layout and scheduling optimisation.
entries.code:
from scipy.optimize import dual_annealing
res = dual_annealing(cost, bounds)

entries.name: Tabu Search / Hill Climbing
entries.why: Local search methods; tabu search forbids recently visited moves to avoid cycling.
entries.example: Timetabling; job-shop scheduling.
entries.code:
best = x
for it in range(N):
    cand = max((n for n in neighbours(x) if n not in tabu), key=f)
    tabu.append(cand); x = cand; best = max(best, x, key=f)

entries.name: CMA-ES
entries.why: Evolution strategy that adapts a full covariance matrix of the search distribution; top black-box optimiser for continuous problems.
entries.example: Optimising robot gaits or controller parameters in simulation.
entries.code:
import cma
es = cma.CMAEvolutionStrategy(x0, 0.5)
es.optimize(objective)

entries.name: NEAT (NeuroEvolution of Augmenting Topologies)
entries.why: Evolves both weights and structure of neural networks.
entries.example: Game-playing agents; evolving small controllers.
entries.code:

pop = neat.Population(neat.Config(neat.DefaultGenome, neat.DefaultReproduction,

entries.name: Multi-Objective Optimisation (NSGA-II)
entries.why: Evolves a Pareto front of trade-off solutions for several conflicting objectives.
entries.example: Trading cost vs. strength in design; accuracy vs. latency of models.
entries.code:
from pymoo.algorithms.moo.nsga2 import NSGA2
from pymoo.optimize import minimize
res = minimize(problem, NSGA2(pop_size=100), ("n_gen", 200))

entries.name: Linear & Integer Programming
entries.why: Optimise a linear objective under linear constraints; integer variables for discrete decisions.
entries.example: Production planning; machine allocation; shift scheduling.
entries.code:
from scipy.optimize import linprog
res = linprog(c, A_ub=A, b_ub=b, bounds=[(0, None)] * len(c))

entries.name: Constraint Satisfaction (CP-SAT)
entries.why: Finds assignments satisfying many logical constraints; very strong for scheduling.
entries.example: Exam timetabling; lab-slot allocation.
entries.code:

m = cp_model.CpModel(); x = m.NewIntVar(0, 10, "x"); m.Add(x + 2 > 5)

entries.name: Hungarian Algorithm (Assignment Problem)
entries.why: Optimal one-to-one assignment minimising total cost in polynomial time.
entries.example: Matching detections to tracks; assigning tasks to robots.
entries.code:
from scipy.optimize import linear_sum_assignment
rows, cols = linear_sum_assignment(cost_matrix)

entries.name: Travelling Salesman / Vehicle Routing Solvers
entries.why: Find short tours or routes visiting all locations (heuristics, OR-Tools).
entries.example: Delivery routing; inspection drone tour planning.

from ortools.constraint_solver import pywrapcp
manager = pywrapcp.RoutingIndexManager(n, n_vehicles, depot)
routing = pywrapcp.RoutingModel(manager)

entries.name: Confusion Matrix, Precision, Recall, F1
entries.why: Core classification metrics; precision = correct among predicted positives, recall = found among actual positives.
entries.example: Reporting defect-detector performance.
entries.code:
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, confusion_matrix
print(classification_report(y_true, y_pred)); cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)

entries.name: ROC-AUC / PR-AUC
entries.why: Threshold-independent ranking quality; PR-AUC is more informative for rare positives.
entries.example: Comparing anomaly detectors.
entries.code:
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, average_precision_score
auc = roc_auc_score(y, scores); ap = average_precision_score(y, scores)

entries.name: mAP (mean Average Precision) for Detection
entries.why: Average precision across classes and IoU thresholds; the standard detection metric (COCO mAP@0.5:0.95).
entries.example: Comparing YOLO models on your dataset.
entries.code:
from ultralytics import YOLO
metrics = YOLO("best.pt").val(data="data.yaml"); print(metrics.box.map, metrics.box.map50)

entries.name: IoU / Dice Metrics for Segmentation
entries.why: Overlap between predicted and true masks; mean IoU across classes for semantic segmentation.
entries.example: Evaluating crack or leaf segmentation.
entries.code: iou = (pred & gt).sum() / (pred | gt).sum()

entries.name: Regression Metrics (RMSE, MAE, R-squared, MAPE)
entries.why: Measure prediction error size and explained variance.
entries.example: Evaluating forecasting and RUL models.
entries.code:
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error, r2_score
rmse = mean_squared_error(y, p) ** 0.5; mae = mean_absolute_error(y, p); r2 = r2_score(y, p)

entries.name: Feature Importance (Impurity & Permutation)
entries.why: Shows which features a model relies on; permutation importance measures the score drop when a feature is shuffled.
entries.example: Explaining which sensor drives failure predictions.
entries.code:
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
r = permutation_importance(model, X_val, y_val, n_repeats=10)

entries.name: Partial Dependence & ICE Plots
entries.why: Show how predictions change as one feature varies, on average (PDP) or per sample (ICE).
entries.example: How does temperature affect predicted failure probability?
entries.code:
from sklearn.inspection import PartialDependenceDisplay
PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator(model, X, features=["temperature"], kind="both")

entries.name: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations)
entries.why: Game-theory attribution of each feature's contribution to each prediction; consistent local and global explanations.
entries.example: Explaining credit or failure predictions from XGBoost.
entries.code:
import shap
explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(model)
shap.summary_plot(explainer.shap_values(X), X)

entries.name: LIME
entries.why: Fits a simple interpretable model around one prediction by perturbing the input.
entries.example: Explaining a single text or image classification.
entries.code:
from lime.lime_tabular import LimeTabularExplainer
exp = LimeTabularExplainer(X_train, feature_names=names).explain_instance(X_test[0],
    model.predict_proba)

entries.name: Grad-CAM / Grad-CAM++
entries.why: Heatmap of image regions that most influenced a CNN's decision, from gradients of the last conv layer.
entries.example: Checking that a leaf-disease classifier looks at lesions, not background.
entries.code:
from pytorch_grad_cam import GradCAM
cam = GradCAM(model=model, target_layers=[model.layer4[-1]])
heatmap = cam(input_tensor=x)[0]

entries.name: Integrated Gradients / Saliency Maps
entries.why: Attribute predictions to input pixels or tokens by integrating gradients from a baseline.
entries.example: Explaining medical image or text predictions.
entries.code:
from captum.attr import IntegratedGradients
attr = IntegratedGradients(model).attribute(x, target=label)

entries.name: Attention Rollout (Transformer Explainability)
entries.why: Combines attention maps across layers to show which input tokens or patches the output depends on.
entries.example: Visualising what a ViT attends to.
entries.code:
rollout = torch.eye(n)
for A in attentions: rollout = (0.5 * A.mean(1) + 0.5 * torch.eye(n)) @ rollout

entries.name: Counterfactual Explanations
entries.why: Finds the smallest input change that would flip the model's decision.
entries.example: "Loan would be approved if income were 10% higher."
entries.code:
import dice_ml
exp = dice_ml.Dice(data, model).generate_counterfactuals(query, total_CFs=3, desired_class="opposite")

entries.name: Monte Carlo Dropout (Uncertainty)
entries.why: Keeps dropout on at test time and averages many passes; the spread estimates model uncertainty.
entries.example: Flagging low-confidence predictions for human review.
entries.code:
model.train()
preds = torch.stack([model(x) for _ in range(30)]); mean, std = preds.mean(0), preds.std(0)

entries.name: Deep Ensembles
entries.why: Train several networks with different seeds; disagreement measures uncertainty. Simple and very reliable.
entries.example: Safety-critical perception.
entries.code: preds = torch.stack([m(x).softmax(-1) for m in models]); uncertainty = preds.var(0).sum(-1)

entries.name: Conformal Prediction
entries.why: Wraps any model to give prediction sets or intervals with guaranteed coverage (e.g. 90%).
entries.example: Reliable prediction intervals for forecasts or classification.
entries.code:

mapie = MapieRegressor(model).fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred, y_int = mapie.predict(X_test, alpha=0.1)

entries.why: Detect inputs unlike the training data, so the model can refuse to predict.

entries.why: Small crafted perturbations can fool networks; training on them improves robustness.

entries.name: Federated Learning (FedAvg / FedProx)
